01-enzymes.q: An enzyme is best described as…
options: a living organism that digests food
01-enzymes.explain: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions without being used up — biological catalysts.

01-enzymes.q: A catalyst…
options: is used up during the reaction
increases the rate of a reaction and is not used up
01-enzymes.explain: Both halves are needed for the two-mark definition: increases the rate, not used up.

01-enzymes.q: Enzymes are made of…
01-enzymes.explain: Enzymes are proteins, which is why heat and pH can change their shape.

01-enzymes.q: The part of an enzyme that the substrate binds to is the…
01-enzymes.explain: The active site has a shape complementary to the substrate.

01-enzymes.q: Why does each enzyme act on only one substrate?
options: Enzymes are too small to hold more than one
Only one substrate has a shape complementary to the active site
Each enzyme is used up after one reaction
01-enzymes.explain: This is specificity — the lock-and-key fit.

01-enzymes.q: When a substrate is bound in the active site, the structure formed is called…
01-enzymes.explain: Enzyme + substrate bound together = enzyme–substrate complex.

01-enzymes.q: What happens to an enzyme at the end of the reaction it catalyses?
options: It is broken down into amino acids
It becomes part of the product
It is unchanged and can be used again
01-enzymes.explain: A catalyst is not used up.

01-enzymes.q: Increasing the temperature from 10 °C to 30 °C speeds up an enzyme reaction because the molecules…
options: have more kinetic energy and collide more often
change the shape of the active site
01-enzymes.explain: Below the optimum the explanation is kinetic energy and collision frequency — the answer the 2023 teacher said students left out.

01-enzymes.q: The optimum temperature of most human enzymes is about…
01-enzymes.explain: Body temperature.

01-enzymes.q: Above its optimum temperature, an enzyme stops working because…
options: the substrate becomes too hot to move
01-enzymes.explain: Heat breaks the bonds holding the shape, so the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme is denatured, not dead.

01-enzymes.q: Which word describes an enzyme whose active site has permanently changed shape?
01-enzymes.explain: Denatured — and it does not recover when cooled.

01-enzymes.q: An enzyme is heated to 80 °C and then cooled to 37 °C. It will…
options: work at its normal rate again
not work, because denaturing is permanent
01-enzymes.explain: Denaturing cannot be undone by cooling.

01-enzymes.q: An enzyme kept at 4 °C and then warmed to 37 °C will…
01-enzymes.explain: Cold only slows molecules down; it never changes the shape of the active site.

01-enzymes.q: A rate–temperature graph for an enzyme usually…
options: rises gradually, peaks, then falls steeply
01-enzymes.explain: Gradual rise from kinetic energy, steep fall from denaturing.

01-enzymes.q: Pepsin works in the stomach. Its optimum pH is about…
01-enzymes.explain: The stomach contains hydrochloric acid.

01-enzymes.q: Moving an enzyme to a pH far above its optimum will…
01-enzymes.explain: Too alkaline denatures an enzyme just as too acidic does.

01-enzymes.q: Amylase breaks down starch into…
01-enzymes.explain: Amylase makes maltose. Maltase then makes glucose — two steps.

01-enzymes.q: Maltase breaks down maltose into…
01-enzymes.explain: The second step of starch digestion.

01-enzymes.q: Which enzyme breaks down protein?
01-enzymes.explain: Protease — pepsin is the protease in the stomach.

01-enzymes.q: The products of protein digestion are…
01-enzymes.explain: Proteins are chains of amino acids.

01-enzymes.q: Lipase breaks down lipids into…
01-enzymes.explain: Both products are needed for the mark.

01-enzymes.q: Which substance digests fat?
01-enzymes.explain: Asked as a one-mark table gap in Year 10 2024 Q1(c).

01-enzymes.q: Why can humans not release energy from cellulose?
options: Cellulose is denatured by stomach acid
01-enzymes.explain: Only cellulase has an active site that fits cellulose.

01-enzymes.q: Cellulase digests cellulose into…
01-enzymes.explain: The glucose is then used in respiration — the Year 11 January 2023 mock chain.

01-enzymes.q: Iodine solution turns blue-black in the presence of…
01-enzymes.explain: Iodine is the starch test.

01-enzymes.q: In the amylase practical, the reaction is complete when the iodine…
01-enzymes.explain: Orange-brown means no starch left.

01-enzymes.q: In an amylase experiment, a shorter time for the starch to disappear means…
01-enzymes.explain: Rate and time are inversely related.

01-enzymes.q: Starch disappears in 40 s at pH 6, 20 s at pH 7 and 55 s at pH 8. The optimum pH is about…
01-enzymes.explain: The shortest time is the fastest rate.

01-enzymes.q: In an investigation into the effect of pH on amylase, the independent variable is…
01-enzymes.explain: The thing you change.

01-enzymes.q: In an investigation into the effect of pH on amylase, the water bath is used to…
01-enzymes.explain: Temperature is a control variable here.

01-enzymes.q: Which is a valid control variable in an enzyme and temperature experiment?
options: Time taken for starch to disappear
01-enzymes.explain: Temperature is the independent variable and time is the dependent one.

01-enzymes.q: Why are samples taken every 10 seconds in the amylase practical?
options: To find the time when starch is no longer present
01-enzymes.explain: Regular sampling pins down when digestion finished.

01-enzymes.q: A reaction stops although temperature and pH are unchanged. The most likely reason is that…
options: the substrate has been used up
01-enzymes.explain: No conditions changed, so do not reach for denaturing.

01-enzymes.q: All the active sites are occupied and the rate is at its maximum. Which change would increase the rate?
01-enzymes.explain: The enzyme is the limiting factor.

01-enzymes.q: The chemical reactions in living cells, controlled by enzymes, are called…
01-enzymes.explain: Metabolism.

01-enzymes.q: Snails grow faster at 23 °C than at 8 °C. The best explanation is…
options: molecules have more kinetic energy so collisions are more frequent
01-enzymes.explain: The 2023 scheme rewarded kinetic energy and collisions; the teacher warned against the 'optimum loop'.

01-enzymes.q: Bile helps pancreatic enzymes work in the small intestine by…
01-enzymes.explain: Pancreatic enzymes have an alkaline optimum.

01-enzymes.q: In a six-mark investigation design, 'keep everything else the same' scores…
options: nothing — each control must be named
01-enzymes.explain: Name them: temperature, volume of amylase, mass of starch.

01-enzymes.q: Which statement about denaturing is correct?
options: The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
The substrate changes shape to fit
01-enzymes.explain: Be specific: the active site.

01-enzymes.q: In the mock scheme for the vinegar investigation, which word for the starch was ignored?
01-enzymes.explain: 'Amount' is too vague. Say mass or volume.

02-photosynthesis.q: Which is the word equation for photosynthesis?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Carbon dioxide and water are the reactants; glucose and oxygen the products. The first option is respiration.

02-photosynthesis.q: Which is the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Six of each small molecule balance one glucose. The last option is respiration.

02-photosynthesis.q: Where in a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll. Mitochondria are for respiration.

02-photosynthesis.q: What is the job of chlorophyll?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light.

02-photosynthesis.q: Which element is needed to make chlorophyll?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Magnesium ions are needed for chlorophyll; without them leaves turn yellow.

02-photosynthesis.q: In photosynthesis, light energy is converted into…
02-photosynthesis.explain: The energy is stored as chemical energy in glucose.

02-photosynthesis.q: Photosynthesis is described as endothermic because it…
02-photosynthesis.explain: It takes in light energy from the surroundings.

02-photosynthesis.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT animal cells?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Cell wall, chloroplasts and permanent vacuole are plant-only.

02-photosynthesis.q: What is a plant cell wall made of?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Cellulose, made from glucose.

02-photosynthesis.q: Why do plants store glucose as starch?
options: Starch is insoluble so it does not affect osmosis
02-photosynthesis.explain: Insoluble starch does not draw water into cells by osmosis.

02-photosynthesis.q: In what form is sugar transported in the phloem?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Sucrose is the transport sugar.

02-photosynthesis.q: Plants need nitrate ions to make…
02-photosynthesis.explain: Nitrate supplies the nitrogen in amino acids.

02-photosynthesis.q: A limiting factor is…
options: the factor in shortest supply that limits the rate
any factor that kills the plant
02-photosynthesis.explain: Whatever is in shortest supply holds the rate back.

02-photosynthesis.q: Which is NOT a limiting factor of photosynthesis?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Oxygen is a product, not one of the three limiting factors.

02-photosynthesis.q: On a graph of rate against light intensity, the line levels off. This is because…
options: another factor, such as CO₂ concentration, is now limiting
02-photosynthesis.explain: Light is no longer limiting — name another factor.

02-photosynthesis.q: Where the rate rises with light intensity, the limiting factor is…
02-photosynthesis.explain: If more light gives a faster rate, light was limiting.

02-photosynthesis.q: Why does the rate of photosynthesis fall at very high temperatures?
02-photosynthesis.explain: The active sites of the enzymes change shape.

02-photosynthesis.q: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm from a plant. The light intensity becomes…
02-photosynthesis.explain: Inverse square law: 1 ÷ 2² = 1/4.

02-photosynthesis.q: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 30 cm. The light intensity becomes…
Which layer of the leaf contains the most chloroplasts?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts near the top of the leaf.

02-photosynthesis.q: What is the function of the air spaces in the spongy mesophyll?
options: To give a large surface area for gas exchange
02-photosynthesis.explain: Gases diffuse through the air spaces into the cells.

02-photosynthesis.q: What controls the opening and closing of stomata?
02-photosynthesis.explain: A pair of guard cells surrounds each stoma.

02-photosynthesis.q: Why is the waxy cuticle important?
02-photosynthesis.explain: It is waterproof; it is also transparent.

02-photosynthesis.q: Why are leaves thin?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Gases only have to diffuse a short way.

02-photosynthesis.q: Closing the stomata reduces photosynthesis because…
02-photosynthesis.explain: CO₂ enters through the stomata.

02-photosynthesis.q: Transpiration is…
options: the uptake of water by roots
the loss of water vapour from the leaves
the movement of sugar in the phloem
02-photosynthesis.explain: Water evaporates and diffuses out through the stomata.

02-photosynthesis.q: Water enters root hair cells by…
02-photosynthesis.explain: Water moves by osmosis; mineral ions often by active transport.

02-photosynthesis.q: Which vessels carry water up the plant?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Xylem carries water and minerals upwards.

02-photosynthesis.q: Which condition would slow down transpiration?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Humid air means a smaller concentration gradient for water vapour.

02-photosynthesis.q: In the dark, a plant…
options: respires, so there is a net release of CO₂
02-photosynthesis.explain: Respiration never stops.

02-photosynthesis.q: At the compensation point…
options: the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration
02-photosynthesis.explain: There is no net gas exchange.

02-photosynthesis.q: In bright light there is a net uptake of CO₂ because…
02-photosynthesis.explain: The plant still respires; photosynthesis uses CO₂ faster.

02-photosynthesis.q: Hydrogencarbonate indicator turns yellow when carbon dioxide…
02-photosynthesis.explain: Yellow = high CO₂; purple = low CO₂.

02-photosynthesis.q: A leaf in bright light in hydrogencarbonate indicator turns it…
02-photosynthesis.explain: Photosynthesis removes CO₂, so the indicator turns purple.

02-photosynthesis.q: In the pondweed experiment, why is sodium hydrogencarbonate added to the water?
02-photosynthesis.explain: It releases CO₂, so CO₂ is not limiting.

02-photosynthesis.q: In the pondweed experiment, the bubbles given off are…
02-photosynthesis.explain: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis.

02-photosynthesis.q: Why is a plant destarched before a starch test experiment?
options: So any starch found was made during the experiment
02-photosynthesis.explain: Old starch would give a false positive.

02-photosynthesis.q: Why is a leaf boiled in ethanol in the starch test?
02-photosynthesis.explain: Removing the green makes the iodine colour visible.

02-photosynthesis.q: Iodine turns blue-black in the presence of…
02-photosynthesis.explain: Iodine is orange-brown; blue-black shows starch.

02-photosynthesis.q: A variegated leaf is used to show that photosynthesis needs…
02-photosynthesis.explain: Only the green parts, with chlorophyll, make starch.

03-respiration.q: What is respiration?
options: Breathing air in and out of the lungs
A reaction that makes energy from oxygen
The exchange of gases in the alveoli
A chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose
03-respiration.explain: Respiration happens in cells and releases energy stored in glucose. Breathing and gas exchange are ventilation, and energy is never made.

03-respiration.q: Which organisms respire?
options: All living organisms, all the time
Animals, and plants only at night
03-respiration.explain: Every living cell respires continuously. Plants respire in the day too — photosynthesis just hides it.

03-respiration.q: Which is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
03-respiration.explain: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and gives carbon dioxide and water. Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen is photosynthesis.

03-respiration.q: Which is the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration?
03-respiration.explain: Six of each small molecule balance one glucose. The unbalanced version scores only one of two marks.

03-respiration.q: In which organelle does aerobic respiration take place?
03-respiration.explain: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts are for photosynthesis.

03-respiration.q: Which molecule provides energy directly for cell processes?
03-respiration.explain: Energy released in respiration is used to make ATP, and ATP supplies the energy to the cell's processes.

03-respiration.q: What is the word equation for anaerobic respiration in human muscle?
03-respiration.explain: In animals there is one product only: lactic acid. No carbon dioxide, no oxygen used.

03-respiration.q: What is the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast?
03-respiration.explain: Yeast and plants make ethanol and carbon dioxide. This is fermentation.

03-respiration.q: Which of these processes uses energy released by respiration?
options: Diffusion of oxygen into the blood
03-respiration.explain: Diffusion, osmosis and evaporation are passive. Muscle contraction needs energy from ATP.

03-respiration.q: Compared with aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration…
options: releases more energy per glucose molecule
releases less energy per glucose molecule
03-respiration.explain: Anaerobic respiration breaks glucose down only partly, so much less energy is released.

03-respiration.q: Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy than aerobic respiration?
options: It takes place in the mitochondria
03-respiration.explain: Energy is left locked in the product — lactic acid or ethanol.

03-respiration.q: What is the oxygen debt?
options: The oxygen breathed out after exercise
The oxygen missed during a race, breathed in later to make up
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid
03-respiration.explain: The extra oxygen is used to break down the lactic acid made by anaerobic respiration.

03-respiration.q: Why do muscles respire anaerobically during a sprint?
options: Oxygen cannot be supplied to them fast enough
Lactic acid is needed for contraction
03-respiration.explain: Aerobic respiration continues, but it cannot meet the demand, so anaerobic respiration tops it up.

03-respiration.q: What causes muscle fatigue during hard exercise?
03-respiration.explain: Lactic acid from anaerobic respiration builds up in the muscles and causes fatigue and cramp.

03-respiration.q: Bread dough rises because yeast produces…
03-respiration.explain: Carbon dioxide bubbles make the dough rise. The ethanol evaporates when it is baked.

03-respiration.q: Which sentence would a mark scheme accept?
03-respiration.explain: Energy cannot be created. Mark schemes reject produces, makes and creates.

03-respiration.q: What happens to limewater when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it?
03-respiration.explain: Limewater turns milky or cloudy with carbon dioxide.

03-respiration.q: Hydrogencarbonate indicator starts orange. What colour does it turn when the carbon dioxide level rises?
03-respiration.explain: More carbon dioxide turns it yellow. Less carbon dioxide turns it purple.

03-respiration.q: In the respiring seeds practical, why is a flask of boiled seeds set up?
options: As a control, because dead seeds cannot respire
To make the seeds germinate faster
To kill microorganisms on the living seeds
03-respiration.explain: The boiled seeds show that the temperature rise needs living, respiring seeds.

03-respiration.q: Why are the seeds rinsed in disinfectant?
options: To kill microorganisms that would respire and release heat
03-respiration.explain: Microbes on the seeds respire too. Without disinfectant the control flask could warm up.

03-respiration.q: Why is a vacuum flask used in the respiring seeds practical?
options: To reduce heat loss to the surroundings
03-respiration.explain: The flask insulates, so the small amount of heat released can be measured.

03-respiration.q: What is the soda lime for in a respirometer?
03-respiration.explain: With carbon dioxide absorbed, the movement of the drop measures oxygen uptake only.

03-respiration.q: The coloured drop in a respirometer moves towards the organisms. Why?
options: They take in oxygen and the carbon dioxide they release is absorbed
The soda lime gives off a gas
03-respiration.explain: The gas volume falls, so the pressure falls and the drop is pulled towards the organisms.

03-respiration.q: How can the temperature of a respirometer be kept constant?
options: Heat it with a Bunsen burner
Stand it in a water bath
03-respiration.explain: A water bath keeps the temperature steady. The real mark scheme ignored Bunsen alone.

03-respiration.q: A respirometer drop moves 14 mm, 17 mm and 17 mm in three repeats. What is the mean?
Why is a layer of oil poured over yeast in glucose solution?
03-respiration.explain: Keeping oxygen out forces the yeast to respire anaerobically.

03-respiration.q: Why is glucose solution boiled and cooled before yeast is added?
options: To make the glucose dissolve faster
03-respiration.explain: Boiling drives out dissolved oxygen. It is cooled so the heat does not kill the yeast.

03-respiration.q: Yeast releases carbon dioxide faster at 30 °C than at 20 °C. Why?
options: Molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more often
03-respiration.explain: Below the optimum, more kinetic energy means more enzyme–substrate collisions and faster respiration.

03-respiration.q: At 70 °C, yeast releases almost no carbon dioxide. Why?
options: The enzymes denature and their active sites change shape
The molecules have too little kinetic energy
03-respiration.explain: Above the optimum, enzymes denature. The substrate no longer fits the active site.

03-respiration.q: A fish in water with little oxygen becomes less active. Which is the best explanation?
options: Less aerobic respiration, so less energy is released
03-respiration.explain: Less oxygen means less aerobic respiration, not none. Say energy is released, not produced.

03-respiration.q: Where in a cell does anaerobic respiration take place?
03-respiration.explain: Anaerobic respiration happens in the cytoplasm. Aerobic respiration happens in the mitochondria.

03-respiration.q: Which gas is a product of aerobic respiration and of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
03-respiration.explain: Both give off carbon dioxide. Anaerobic respiration in animals does not.

03-respiration.q: Bacteria in yoghurt respire anaerobically. Which product makes the milk acidic?
03-respiration.explain: The bacteria make lactic acid, like animal muscle. Less oxygen means more of it, faster.

03-respiration.q: How is the aerobic respiration equation related to the photosynthesis equation?
03-respiration.explain: Respiration uses glucose and oxygen; photosynthesis makes them. The equations are mirror images.

03-respiration.q: Which cell would you expect to contain the most mitochondria?
03-respiration.explain: Muscle cells need a lot of energy. Red blood cells and xylem vessels have none.

03-respiration.q: Ethanol made by anaerobic respiration can be burned as a fuel. What does this show?
options: Energy is still stored in the product
03-respiration.explain: If anaerobic respiration released all the energy, there would be none left in the ethanol to burn.

03-respiration.q: When do plants respire?
options: All the time, day and night
03-respiration.explain: All living cells respire all the time. In bright light photosynthesis is just faster.

03-respiration.q: Roots in waterlogged soil respire anaerobically. Why?
options: Water has replaced the air in the soil
03-respiration.explain: With no air in the soil, there is too little oxygen for aerobic respiration.

03-respiration.q: In the carbon cycle, which process returns carbon dioxide to the air from all living organisms?
03-respiration.explain: Every living thing respires. Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air.

03-respiration.q: A student writes: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. What is wrong?
options: Energy is not a substance, so it is not a product
The product should be lactic acid
03-respiration.explain: Energy is released, but it is not a chemical product. Leave it out of the word equation.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: In what order does air pass into the lungs?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: The tubes branch from large to small: trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, then the alveoli.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Where does gas exchange take place in the lungs?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Only the alveoli have the thin walls and blood supply for gas exchange.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What holds the trachea open?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Cartilage rings stop the trachea collapsing when the pressure inside falls.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What does the diaphragm do when you breathe in?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: The diaphragm is domed at rest. Contracting pulls it down and flat. Collapses was rejected by the school.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What do the intercostal muscles do when you breathe in?
options: Relax, moving the ribs up and out
Contract, moving the ribs down and in
Contract, moving the ribs up and out
Relax, moving the ribs down and in
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Contracting intercostals lift the ribcage up and out, increasing the volume.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What happens to the pressure in the thorax when you breathe in?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: The volume increases, so the pressure falls, and air moves in from outside.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Which is the correct order of events when breathing in?
options: Muscles contract → volume increases → pressure decreases → air moves in
Pressure decreases → volume increases → muscles contract → air moves in
Air moves in → volume increases → pressure decreases
Muscles relax → volume decreases → air moves in
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Muscles first, then volume, then pressure, then air. Each step is its own mark.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What is the role of the pleural fluid?
options: It reduces friction as the lungs move
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: The fluid between the pleural membranes lets the lungs slide smoothly against the chest wall.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Which happens when you breathe out at rest?
options: The diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards
The intercostal muscles contract and lift the ribs
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Breathing out is the reverse of breathing in: the muscles relax and the volume decreases.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: By which process do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the alveolus wall?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Gases move down their concentration gradients by diffusion. Ventilation is breathing.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Which feature of the alveoli gives a short diffusion distance?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Thin walls mean the gases have only a short way to diffuse.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: How does a dense network of capillaries help gas exchange?
options: It increases the surface area only
It makes the alveolus walls thinner
It maintains a steep concentration gradient
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Blood flow keeps carrying oxygen away and bringing carbon dioxide, so the gradient stays steep.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Why is the lining of the alveoli moist?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Oxygen dissolves in the moisture, then diffuses across the wall.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What do millions of alveoli provide?
options: A large surface area for diffusion
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Many tiny sacs give a huge total surface area, so more gas can diffuse at once.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Roughly what percentage of exhaled air is oxygen?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Exhaled air still has about 16% oxygen, down from about 21% in inhaled air.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Roughly what percentage of exhaled air is carbon dioxide?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Carbon dioxide rises from about 0.04% to about 4%.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Why is the percentage of nitrogen the same in inhaled and exhaled air?
options: It is not used by the body
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Nitrogen is breathed in and out unchanged. The school's scheme gave a mark for saying it is not used.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Why does exhaled air contain more oxygen than the air in the alveoli?
options: Oxygen is made in the lungs
The blood releases oxygen into the alveoli
It mixes with air from the airways, where no gas exchange happens
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Gas exchange only happens at the alveoli. Air from the trachea and bronchi still has plenty of oxygen.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: A student breathes in through one limewater flask and out through another. What happens in the flask they breathe out through?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Exhaled air has more carbon dioxide, so its limewater turns milky faster.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What is the job of the cilia in the airways?
options: To trap dust in sticky fluid
To sweep mucus up and out of the airways
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Mucus traps the dirt and bacteria; the cilia sweep it away.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Which effect is caused by tar in cigarette smoke?
options: Damage to cilia and lung cancer
Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Tar is a carcinogen and destroys cilia. Addiction and heart rate are nicotine; oxygen capacity is carbon monoxide.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: How does carbon monoxide affect the body?
options: It binds to haemoglobin, reducing the oxygen the blood can carry
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Carbon monoxide takes the place of oxygen on haemoglobin. Poisons the blood scores nothing.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Which describes nicotine?
options: A carcinogen that causes lung cancer
Addictive, and raises the heart rate
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Nicotine is the addictive drug in tobacco. It raises heart rate and blood pressure.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What is emphysema?
options: An increase in the number of cilia
Breakdown of alveolus walls, reducing the surface area
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: The alveoli merge into fewer, larger spaces, so the surface area for gas exchange falls.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: A person with emphysema is breathless when exercising. Why?
options: Less oxygen diffuses into the blood, so less respiration in the muscles
Their alveoli have more surface area
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Smaller surface area, less oxygen in, less aerobic respiration, less energy released.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: How does smoking increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
options: Fatty deposits build up and narrow the coronary arteries
Cilia in the heart are destroyed
The lungs press on the heart
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Narrowed coronary arteries mean less oxygen reaches the heart muscle.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Why do smokers get more chest infections?
options: Carbon monoxide kills white blood cells
Mucus containing bacteria is not swept out of the lungs
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Tar damages the cilia, so mucus and the bacteria in it stay in the airways.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Babies of mothers who smoke tend to have a lower birth mass. Why?
options: Less oxygen reaches the fetus, so less respiration for growth
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen the mother's blood carries, so less reaches the fetus.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Why does breathing rate increase during exercise?
options: To supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide faster
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Muscles respire faster, needing more oxygen and making more carbon dioxide.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Why does breathing stay fast for a while after exercise?
options: To repay the oxygen debt — lactic acid must be broken down
Because carbon dioxide levels are low
Because the muscles are still contracting hard
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid made during exercise.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: In a practical on exercise and breathing, what is the dependent variable?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: The dependent variable is what you measure: the breathing rate.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Which is a control variable in the exercise and breathing practical?
options: Whether the person is resting or exercising
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: The length of the exercise must be kept the same. Resting or exercising is the independent variable.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: How could a student make the breathing-rate results more reliable?
options: Use a different exercise each time
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Repeats and a mean improve reliability. The school rejected more speeds and different ages.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: A person's ventilation rate is 36 dm³ per minute at 12 breaths per minute. What is the volume of each breath?
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Volume per breath = ventilation rate ÷ breathing rate = 36 ÷ 12 = 3 dm³.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What is 65 dm³ in cm³?
What is vital capacity?
options: The volume of air breathed in at rest
The maximum volume of air that can be breathed out in one breath
The volume of the lungs at rest
The number of breaths per minute
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Vital capacity is the most you can force out after the deepest breath in.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Why does vital capacity fall in old age?
options: The breathing muscles weaken and the lungs become less elastic
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Weaker intercostal muscles and diaphragm, and stiffer lungs, mean less air can be forced out.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: Why might a scientist use the median rather than the mean?
options: It is less affected by extreme values
It is always larger than the mean
It uses only the largest value
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: The median is the middle value, so a few very high or low readings do not drag it.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: What is the difference between breathing and respiration?
options: Breathing moves air; respiration releases energy in cells
Respiration moves air; breathing releases energy
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Breathing is ventilation. Respiration is a chemical reaction in every cell.

04-gas-exchange-in-humans.q: A student writes: the diaphragm collapses when you breathe in. What should they write?
options: The diaphragm contracts and flattens, moving down
The diaphragm contracts and moves up
The diaphragm is pulled down by the lungs
04-gas-exchange-in-humans.explain: Contracts and flattens is the wording that scores. The lungs cannot pull anything.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Why do large animals need a transport system?
options: They have a large surface area to volume ratio
They have a small surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion is too slow
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Most cells in a large animal are far from any surface. Diffusion over that distance would be too slow.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What is meant by a double circulatory system?
options: There are two types of blood
Blood flows both ways in each vessel
Blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: One loop goes to the lungs, the other to the body, and both pass through the heart.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What is the advantage of a double circulation?
options: Blood is pumped again after the lungs, so it reaches the body at high pressure
The lungs get blood at very high pressure
The heart can beat more slowly
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Returning to the heart after the lungs lets the blood be re-pressurised before going to the body.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Which side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs?
options: Neither — the lungs pull it in
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The right side pumps to the lungs; the left side pumps to the body.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Which vessel brings deoxygenated blood from the body to the heart?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The vena cava empties into the right atrium.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What does the pulmonary vein carry?
options: Deoxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart
Oxygenated blood from the heart to the body
Oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: It is a vein, so it goes to the heart, and it carries blood just oxygenated in the lungs.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Through which vessel does blood leave the left ventricle?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The aorta carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Which is the correct definition of an artery?
options: A vessel carrying blood away from the heart
A vessel carrying blood towards the heart
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Arteries are defined by direction. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker wall than the right?
options: It pumps blood to the lungs
It pumps blood at higher pressure around the whole body
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Wall thickness is about pressure, not oxygen. The school called the oxygen answer a common error.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What is the job of the valves in the heart?
options: To add oxygen to the blood
To separate the left and right sides
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Valves close when blood tries to flow the wrong way. The septum separates the sides.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What is the septum?
options: A valve between an atrium and a ventricle
The artery that supplies the heart muscle
The wall that keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart
The chamber that pumps blood to the lungs
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The septum divides the left side of the heart from the right.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What type of tissue makes up most of the heart wall?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The heart wall is cardiac muscle, which contracts without tiring.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What do the coronary arteries do?
options: Carry blood from the gut to the liver
Supply the heart muscle with oxygen and glucose
Drain blood from the heart muscle
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The heart muscle needs its own blood supply. Coronary veins drain it.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: How does a stent help a person with coronary heart disease?
options: It keeps the coronary artery open
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Keeping the artery open lets blood and oxygen reach the heart muscle.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Which is NOT a risk factor for coronary heart disease?
options: A diet high in saturated fat
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Exercise lowers the risk. It lowers blood pressure and strengthens the heart.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What effect does adrenaline have on the heart?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Adrenaline speeds up the heart, sending more oxygen and glucose to the muscles.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Which glands release adrenaline?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The adrenal glands release adrenaline in fight or flight situations.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Why does heart rate increase during exercise?
options: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose delivered faster
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Faster respiration in muscles needs faster delivery of oxygen and glucose, and faster removal of carbon dioxide.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Which type of blood vessel has valves?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Blood in veins is at low pressure, so valves stop it flowing backwards.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What is the wall of a capillary like?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: One cell thick gives a short diffusion distance to the tissues.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Why do arteries have thick, elastic walls?
options: To withstand high pressure from the heart
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Blood leaves the heart at high pressure. Elastic walls stretch and recoil with each beat.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Which vessel carries blood from the intestines to the liver?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The hepatic portal vein carries blood rich in digested food to the liver.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Which organ does the renal artery supply?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Renal means kidney. Hepatic means liver.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What are the four components of blood?
options: Red blood cells, white blood cells, haemoglobin and water
Red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and plasma
Red blood cells, antibodies, glucose and urea
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Two types of cell, the platelet fragments, and the liquid plasma.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Which substance is carried mainly by red blood cells, not by the plasma?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells. Plasma carries the others.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Between which organs does plasma carry urea?
options: From the kidneys to the liver
From the liver to the kidneys
From the lungs to the kidneys
From the small intestine to the liver
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Urea is made in the liver and removed by the kidneys.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: In the lungs, haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form…
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Oxyhaemoglobin forms where oxygen is high and splits up where oxygen is low.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: How does having no nucleus help a red blood cell?
options: There is more room for haemoglobin
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: More haemoglobin means more oxygen carried per cell.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What does the biconcave shape of a red blood cell give it?
options: A large surface area to volume ratio for fast diffusion of oxygen
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The dimpled disc shape increases the surface for oxygen to diffuse across.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: People living at high altitude have more red blood cells. Why?
options: There is less oxygen in the air, so more haemoglobin is needed to carry enough
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: More red cells and haemoglobin let the blood still pick up enough oxygen.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What does a phagocyte do?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Phagocytes surround a pathogen, hold it in a vesicle and digest it with enzymes.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What does a lymphocyte do?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Lymphocytes release antibodies specific to one pathogen.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What is an antigen?
options: A molecule on a pathogen's surface that is recognised as foreign
A type of white blood cell
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Antibodies are made by lymphocytes to match antigens.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Why is each antibody specific to one pathogen?
options: Its shape is complementary to one antigen
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The antibody only binds to the antigen whose shape matches it.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What does a vaccine contain?
options: A weakened or inactivated pathogen with its antigens
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The antigens trigger lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells, without causing illness.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: Why does vaccination give long-term protection?
options: Antibodies stay in the blood for ever
Memory cells make antibodies sooner, faster and in greater quantity
The pathogen stays in the body harmlessly
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Memory cells respond quickly if the real pathogen arrives, destroying it before you are ill.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What are platelets?
options: Cell fragments that help the blood clot
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Platelets start the reactions that form a clot.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: During clotting, soluble fibrinogen is converted into…
options: insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The fibrin mesh traps red blood cells to form the clot.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: What are the two reasons clotting is important?
options: It raises blood pressure and speeds circulation
It carries oxygen and removes carbon dioxide
It prevents blood loss and stops microorganisms entering
It makes antibodies and memory cells
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: The spec names both: prevent blood loss and prevent entry of microorganisms.

05-heart-circulation-and-blood.q: A drawing of a cell is 50 mm long. The real cell is 0.01 mm long. What is the magnification?
05-heart-circulation-and-blood.explain: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 50 ÷ 0.01 = 5000.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What does the central nervous system consist of?
options: The brain and all the nerves
The spinal cord and sense organs
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. Nerves link it to the rest of the body.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What is an effector?
options: A cell that detects a stimulus
A neurone in the spinal cord
A muscle or gland that carries out a response
A chemical that crosses a synapse
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Receptors detect; effectors respond.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What is a stimulus?
options: A change in the environment that is detected
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The stimulus is the change. The receptor detects it.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Which is the correct order in a reflex arc?
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Sensory in, relay in the middle, motor out.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Where is the relay neurone in a reflex arc?
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The relay neurone sits inside the CNS, linking sensory to motor.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Which way does a sensory neurone carry impulses?
options: From the CNS to an effector
From an effector to a receptor
From a receptor to the CNS
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Sensory neurones carry impulses into the CNS.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Which way does a motor neurone carry impulses?
options: From a receptor to the CNS
From the CNS to an effector
From an effector to a receptor
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Motor neurones carry impulses out to muscles and glands.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Which describes a reflex action?
options: Rapid and automatic, with no conscious thought
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Reflexes happen without you deciding to do them.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What is the main advantage of a reflex?
options: It is fast, so it reduces harm
It lets you think before acting
Its effect lasts a long time
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The short pathway gives a fast response, limiting damage.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What is a synapse?
options: The fatty sheath around a neurone
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: A synapse is a tiny gap crossed by a chemical.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: How does a signal cross a synapse?
options: Ions are pumped by active transport
A neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap
A hormone carries it in the blood
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds to receptors on the next neurone.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Why can impulses cross a synapse in only one direction?
options: Neurotransmitter is released on one side and the receptors are on the other
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Nothing releases transmitter going backwards, and there are no receptors to receive it.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What does the myelin sheath do?
options: Insulates the neurone and speeds up the impulse
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The fatty sheath insulates the long fibre, so impulses travel faster.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Which is true of nervous communication, compared with hormonal?
options: Its signals are carried in the blood
It uses electrical impulses and is fast and short-lived
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Nervous: electrical, fast, short, precise. Hormonal: chemical, in the blood, slower, longer.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: How are hormones carried around the body?
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Hormones are chemicals released into the blood by glands.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What is the difference between a nerve and a neurone?
options: A nerve is a bundle of many neurones
A neurone is a bundle of nerves
Nerves are only found in the brain
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: A neurone is one nerve cell. A nerve is a bundle of them.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: An impulse travels 1.2 m at 80 m/s. How long does it take?
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: time = distance ÷ speed = 1.2 ÷ 80 = 0.015 s.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: How might a painkiller stop a person feeling pain?
options: By speeding up the sensory neurones
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Fewer impulses reach the brain if the synapses are blocked.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Which part of the eye does most of the refraction?
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The cornea bends light the most. The lens fine-tunes the focus.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Where are the receptor cells in the eye?
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Rods and cones are in the retina.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Which structure carries impulses from the eye to the brain?
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The optic nerve connects the retina to the brain.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What does the iris do?
options: Controls the size of the pupil
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The iris contains the circular and radial muscles.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What is the pupil?
options: A hole that lets light into the eye
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The pupil is a gap, not a structure. The iris controls its size.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Which describes cone cells?
options: They detect colour but need bright light
They work in dim light and see only black and white
They are found in the cornea
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Cones need bright light and give colour. Rods work in dim light.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Why do things look grey in dim light?
options: There is not enough light to stimulate the cones
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Only the rods respond in dim light, and rods do not detect colour.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What happens in the iris in bright light?
options: Radial muscles contract and circular muscles relax
Circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Contracting circular muscles make the pupil smaller. Students often get this pair the wrong way round.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What happens to the pupil in dim light?
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Radial muscles contract, widening the pupil to let more light in.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Why does the pupil constrict in bright light?
options: To protect the retina from too much light
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Less light reaches the retina, which prevents damage.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What does antagonistic mean for a pair of muscles?
options: They work in opposition — one contracts as the other relaxes
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The circular and radial muscles of the iris are an antagonistic pair.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: When looking at a near object, the ciliary muscles…
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Contracting makes the ring of ciliary muscle smaller, so the ligaments go slack.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: When looking at a near object, the suspensory ligaments…
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Ligaments are not muscles. The school's scheme did not accept relax — they slacken.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: When looking at a near object, the lens becomes…
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: A fatter lens refracts the light more, which a near object needs.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Which describes focusing on a distant object?
options: Ciliary muscles contract, ligaments slack, lens thick
Ciliary muscles relax, ligaments slack, lens thick
Ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tight, lens thin
Ciliary muscles contract, ligaments tight, lens thin
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Distant light needs little refraction, so the lens is pulled thin.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Why must the lens be thicker to focus on a near object?
options: Less light comes from near objects
Light from a near object needs more refraction
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: More curved means more bending, bringing the light to a focus on the retina.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Why does a long-sighted person see near objects as blurred?
options: Light focuses in front of the retina
Light from near objects focuses behind the retina
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The eyeball is too short or the lens cannot get thick enough.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: How does a cataract affect vision?
options: The cloudy lens lets less light reach the retina
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Less light reaches the retina, so fewer impulses go to the brain.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: An albino rat has an iris with no pigment. What is the effect?
options: The pupil cannot constrict at all
Light passes through the iris, so the pupil cannot control how much light enters
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The iris no longer blocks light, so too much reaches the retina in bright light.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: Why do two forward-facing eyes judge distance better than one?
options: They give an overlapping field of view
They can see behind the head
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Seeing the same area from two angles lets the brain judge distance. Wider view alone is ignored.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: A woodlouse rolls into a ball when touched. Why is this a reflex?
options: It is automatic and does not involve conscious thought
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: The one mark is for automatic, or does not involve thinking.

06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.q: What is homeostasis?
options: Keeping the internal environment of the body constant
06-nervous-system-and-the-eye.explain: Body temperature and water content are examples. It is covered in module 8.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which is the best definition of a hormone?
options: An electrical impulse carried along neurones
A chemical messenger made by an endocrine gland and carried in the blood to a target organ
An enzyme that speeds up reactions in the blood
A chemical released at a synapse
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: All four parts count: chemical, endocrine gland, carried in the blood, target organ. A chemical at a synapse is a neurotransmitter.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Compared with nervous responses, hormonal responses are usually…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Hormones travel in the blood, so they are slower to act, but their effects last longer.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which gland produces adrenaline?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys and release adrenaline.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which organ produces both insulin and glucagon?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Both come from the pancreas. The liver responds to them but does not make them.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which gland releases ADH?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: ADH is released by the pituitary gland in the brain and acts on the kidney.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose concentration?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Insulin lowers blood glucose. Glucagon and adrenaline raise it.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Insulin causes the liver to…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Insulin makes the liver store glucose as glycogen, so blood glucose falls.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: When blood glucose falls too low, the pancreas releases…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Glucagon makes the liver convert glycogen back into glucose. Glycogen is a stored carbohydrate, not a hormone.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Why is insulin injected rather than swallowed?
options: It would be absorbed too quickly
It is a protein, so it would be digested by proteases
It is too acidic for the stomach
It only works in the muscles
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Insulin is a protein. Proteases in the stomach and small intestine would break it down into amino acids.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which is NOT an effect of adrenaline?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Adrenaline increases the breathing rate, to get more oxygen to the muscles.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Why does adrenaline increase the heart rate?
options: To deliver more oxygen and glucose to the muscles for respiration
To make more red blood cells
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: More blood flow means more oxygen and glucose reach the muscles, so more respiration releases more energy.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Why do the pupils dilate when adrenaline is released?
options: To let more light in so danger can be seen
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Wider pupils let more light into the eye, helping you see the danger.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Homeostasis is…
options: the removal of waste products of metabolism
the maintenance of a constant internal environment
a growth response to a stimulus
the release of hormones into the blood
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Homeostasis keeps conditions inside the body, such as temperature and water content, steady.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which two are named in the spec as examples of homeostasis?
options: Body water content and body temperature
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: The spec's two examples are body water content and body temperature. Blood glucose is controlled the same way.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: In negative feedback, a change from the normal level…
options: triggers a response that opposes the change
triggers a response that increases the change
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: The response opposes the change, returning the level to normal. That is why the system is self-correcting.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: When the body is too hot, the arterioles supplying the skin…
options: narrow, so less blood flows near the surface
move closer to the skin surface
widen, so more blood flows near the surface
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: This is vasodilation. Vessels never move; the amount of blood through them changes.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: How does vasodilation help to cool the body?
options: More heat is lost by radiation from blood near the skin surface
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: More warm blood flows close to the surface, so more heat is lost by radiation.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which structures widen during vasodilation?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: It is the arterioles that widen. The school rejected 'capillaries dilate'.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: How does sweating cool the body?
options: Sweat evaporates, taking heat from the skin
Sweat blocks heat from the sun
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Evaporation of the water in sweat takes heat energy from the skin.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: When the body is too cold, vasoconstriction means…
options: more blood flows near the skin
less blood flows near the skin, so less heat is lost
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Arterioles to the skin narrow, so less warm blood is near the surface and less heat is lost.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Shivering helps warm the body because…
options: muscle contraction needs more respiration, which releases heat
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Rapid muscle contractions increase respiration, and respiration releases energy as heat.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: During a long cycle ride, the core temperature rises mainly because…
options: muscles respire more and release heat
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: More muscle contraction means more respiration, which releases energy as heat.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: A tropism is…
options: a growth response towards or away from a stimulus
a fast reflex in a plant
the movement of a whole plant
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Plants respond by growing. Positive means towards the stimulus, negative means away.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: A plant stem growing towards light is an example of…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Towards the stimulus is positive; light is the stimulus, so positive phototropism. This was 2024 Y10 Q1(b).

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Roots growing downwards show…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Roots grow towards gravity, so they are positively gravitropic.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Shoots are…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Shoots grow up, away from gravity, and towards light.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Where is auxin made in a shoot?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Auxin is made at the shoot tip. Cutting off the tip stops bending.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: In a shoot, auxin causes…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Auxin makes cells get longer, not more numerous.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: When light comes from one side, auxin in a shoot…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Auxin collects on the shaded side, giving an unequal distribution.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Why does a shoot bend towards light?
options: Cells on the lit side elongate more
Cells on the shaded side elongate more
Cells on the shaded side die
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: More auxin on the shaded side makes those cells elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: In roots, auxin…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: The opposite of shoots: the side with more auxin grows less, so the root bends down.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: A shoot with its tip covered by an opaque cap does not bend towards light. This shows that…
options: auxin is made in the roots
light is detected at the tip
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: With the tip covered the shoot cannot detect the direction of light, so no unequal distribution forms.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: What is the advantage to a plant of shoots growing towards light?
options: More light is absorbed for photosynthesis
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Leaves facing the light absorb more of it, so the plant can photosynthesise more.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: What is an advantage to a plant of roots growing downwards?
options: They reach water and mineral ions
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Roots growing down reach water and mineral ions and anchor the plant.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Nerve impulses travel at 55 m/s. Hormones travel at 0.07 m/s. The ratio of nerve speed to hormone speed is about…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: 55 ÷ 0.07 = 786, so the ratio is 786 : 1.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which hormone is produced by the testes?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Testosterone, from the testes, controls male secondary sexual characteristics.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which gland produces progesterone?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: The ovaries make oestrogen and progesterone. This was 2022 Edexcel 1B Q1.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Which is a feature of nervous communication but not hormonal?
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Nervous signals are electrical and travel along neurones. The other three describe hormones.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: In type 1 diabetes, the pancreas…
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Too little insulin means blood glucose can rise too high. It is treated with insulin injections.

07-hormones-and-tropisms.q: Why must a person with diabetes monitor how much they exercise?
options: Exercise raises blood glucose too high
Exercise uses glucose, so blood glucose could fall too low
Exercise makes the pancreas release glycogen
07-hormones-and-tropisms.explain: Exercise uses up glucose in respiration. With injected insulin also lowering it, blood glucose could fall too low.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Excretion is…
options: the removal of waste products of metabolism
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Excretion removes substances the body made, such as urea and carbon dioxide. Removing undigested food is egestion.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which is egestion, not excretion?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Faeces are undigested food that was never absorbed, so passing them is egestion.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which organ excretes carbon dioxide?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Carbon dioxide from respiration is excreted by the lungs.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Where is urea made?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids, then excreted by the kidneys.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Urea is made from…
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver. The ammonia formed is converted to urea.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Deamination is the removal of…
options: the amino group from amino acids
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: The amino group is removed in the liver, forming ammonia, which becomes urea.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which tube carries urine from the kidney to the bladder?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: The ureter goes kidney to bladder. The urethra goes bladder to outside.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which is the correct path of urine?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra. Ureter and urethra are the classic swap.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which blood vessel brings blood to the kidney?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: The renal artery brings blood containing urea; the renal vein takes cleaned blood away.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Where does ultrafiltration happen?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Blood at high pressure in the glomerulus is filtered into the Bowman's capsule.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: What causes the high pressure in the glomerulus?
options: The vessel entering is wider than the vessel leaving
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Blood enters more easily than it leaves, so pressure builds up and forces small molecules out.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which substance is NOT normally in the glomerular filtrate?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Proteins are too large to pass out of the glomerulus.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Why are blood cells not found in the filtrate?
options: They are too large to be filtered
They are destroyed in the glomerulus
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Blood cells and proteins are too large. They never leave the blood, so they are never reabsorbed either.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Where is glucose reabsorbed?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: All the glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, the first coiled part.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Glucose is reabsorbed by…
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Active transport moves glucose against the concentration gradient, using energy from respiration.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Why do the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule have many mitochondria?
options: To release energy for active transport
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Active transport needs energy, released by aerobic respiration in the mitochondria.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: In a healthy person, how much of the filtered glucose is reabsorbed?
options: Only what the body needs that day
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: All the glucose is reabsorbed, so normal urine contains none.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which substance is filtered but not reabsorbed at all?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Urea is waste. It stays in the filtrate and leaves in the urine.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Where is water reabsorbed under the control of ADH?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: ADH changes how permeable the collecting duct is. The school scheme wanted the collecting duct named.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Water leaves the collecting duct by…
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Water moves by osmosis into the salty tissue around the duct, then into the blood.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which part of the nephron makes the surrounding tissue salty, so water can be reabsorbed?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: The loop of Henle builds up a high salt concentration around the collecting duct.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: When a person is dehydrated, the pituitary gland releases…
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Blood is too concentrated, so more ADH is released to save water.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: ADH makes the collecting duct…
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: More permeable, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: More ADH in the blood leads to…
options: a large volume of dilute urine
a small volume of concentrated urine
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: More water is reabsorbed, so less urine is made, and it is more concentrated.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Someone drinks a lot of water. Which is correct?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Blood becomes dilute, less ADH is released, less water is reabsorbed, so there is a large volume of dilute urine.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which part of the brain detects the water content of the blood?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: The hypothalamus detects the change; the pituitary gland releases the ADH.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Normal urine contains…
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Spec 2.79B: urine contains water, urea and ions. Glucose and protein should not be there.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Protein in the urine most likely means…
options: the filter in the glomerulus is damaged
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Protein is normally too large to be filtered, so finding it means the filter is letting large molecules through.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Glucose in the urine of an untreated diabetic is caused by…
options: so much glucose being filtered that not all can be reabsorbed
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Blood glucose is very high, so more is filtered than the tubule can reabsorb.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which reagent tests for protein?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Biuret turns from blue to lilac or purple if protein is present.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: A positive Benedict's test for glucose gives…
options: a green, yellow or brick-red colour after heating
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Benedict's must be heated; it changes from blue to green, yellow or brick red.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Urea concentration is 0.3 g/dm³ in the filtrate and 18 g/dm³ in the urine. How many times more concentrated is it in the urine?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: 18 ÷ 0.3 = 60. Water is reabsorbed but urea is not, so urea becomes concentrated.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Why is urea more concentrated in urine than in the filtrate?
options: Urea is added in the collecting duct
Water is reabsorbed but urea is not
Urea is made in the kidney
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Taking water back while leaving urea behind concentrates the urea.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: In dialysis, urea leaves the blood because…
options: the dialysis fluid contains more urea
the dialysis fluid contains no urea, so urea diffuses out
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: There is a concentration gradient from blood to fluid, so urea diffuses out through the partially permeable membrane.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Why does dialysis fluid contain glucose at the normal blood concentration?
options: So there is no net loss of glucose from the blood
To remove glucose from the blood
To make the blood more dilute
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Equal concentrations on both sides mean no net diffusion, so the patient keeps their glucose.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Albumin, a large protein, stays in the blood during dialysis because…
options: it is too large to pass through the membrane
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: The partially permeable membrane has pores too small for large proteins. This was 2022 Y10 Q7.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Why does an athlete who drinks nothing after exercise produce dark urine?
options: Glucose is lost in the urine
More ADH is released, so more water is reabsorbed
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Sweating makes the blood concentrated, so more ADH is released and a small volume of concentrated urine is made.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which organ excretes water, salts and a little urea in sweat?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: The skin excretes these in sweat, though its main job in sweating is cooling.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Controlling the water content of the blood is called…
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: Osmoregulation is one of the kidney's two roles; the other is excretion of urea.

08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.q: Which structure is the cup that collects the filtrate from the glomerulus?
08-homeostasis-and-the-kidney.explain: The Bowman's capsule surrounds the glomerulus and receives the filtrate.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: All the organisms of one species living in a habitat make up a…
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: One species is a population. All the species together are a community.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A community is…
options: the place where an organism lives
all the organisms of one species
all the populations of different species in a habitat
the living and non-living parts of an area
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: A community is every population of every species in the habitat, living things only.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: An ecosystem is…
options: a community and the non-living environment it interacts with
all the living things in an area
all the animals in a habitat
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: An ecosystem includes the non-living part. 'All the living things' is only a community.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A habitat is…
options: the place where an organism lives
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Habitat is the place. The other terms describe groups of organisms or feeding relationships.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Biodiversity is best described as…
options: the number of organisms in an area
the number of different species in an area
the mass of producers in an area
the size of the largest population
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Biodiversity is about how many different species there are, and how evenly spread they are.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Field A has three species in even numbers. Field B has the same three species but one makes up 90% of the plants. Which has greater biodiversity?
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Same number of species, but field A's organisms are spread more evenly, so it is more diverse.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Why are quadrats placed at random coordinates?
options: To avoid bias, so the sample is representative
So every quadrat has the same count
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Choosing where to put them could bias the result. Random placement gives a representative sample.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A 400 m² field is sampled with 0.25 m² quadrats. The mean is 5 plants per quadrat. What is the estimated population?
Why is a mean taken from many quadrats rather than using one?
options: One quadrat is unlikely to be representative
Quadrats are too small to count
The spec says to use ten
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: More quadrats give a more representative sample and a more reliable estimate.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A transect is used to…
options: count every plant in a field
show how distribution changes across a habitat
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Quadrats placed at intervals along a line show how species change with conditions, such as up a beach.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Which is an abiotic factor?
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Abiotic means non-living. The others are effects of living things, so they are biotic.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Which is a biotic factor?
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Competition involves other organisms, so it is biotic.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: What do the arrows in a food chain show?
options: Which organism eats the other, pointing to the food
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Arrows point from the organism eaten to the one eating it, showing energy transfer.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A food chain always begins with a…
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Producers make their own food by photosynthesis and bring energy into the chain.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: In grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the frog is the…
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: It eats the primary consumer, so it is a secondary consumer at trophic level 3.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: In grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the snake is at trophic level…
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Grass 1, grasshopper 2, frog 3, snake 4 — a tertiary consumer.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Decomposers are…
options: bacteria and fungi that break down dead material
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and waste, recycling nutrients.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: How do saprotrophic fungi digest dead material?
options: They swallow it and digest it inside
They secrete enzymes onto it and absorb the products
They wait for bacteria to do it
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Digestion happens outside their cells. They absorb the soluble products and use them in respiration.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: About what percentage of energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: About 10% is transferred; roughly 90% is lost at each step.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Which is NOT a way energy is lost between trophic levels?
options: Parts of the organism not eaten
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Consumers do not photosynthesise. The others are all real losses.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Most of the energy lost between trophic levels leaves as…
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Respiration releases energy, and much of it is lost to the surroundings as heat.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Why are food chains rarely longer than four or five trophic levels?
options: So little energy is left that another level cannot be supported
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: With about 90% lost at each step, very little energy remains after four or five transfers.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Producers have 10.6 kg/m² of biomass and primary consumers 2.4 kg/m². What percentage is transferred?
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: 2.4 ÷ 10.6 × 100 = 22.6%. This appeared in both a school and a real paper.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A snail eats 1.2 g of food and egests 0.3 g. What percentage does it absorb?
Why do herbivores egest a large proportion of what they eat?
options: Plant material such as cellulose is hard to digest
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Much plant material cannot be digested, so it leaves in the faeces.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Why do mammals pass on less of their food energy to the next level than insects do?
options: They respire more to keep warm, losing more heat
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Mammals keep a constant body temperature, so more of their energy is released as heat.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Why does a fox get more energy from a shorter food chain?
options: There are fewer transfers between trophic levels, so less energy is lost
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Each transfer loses energy. The school wanted 'the chain is shorter' as the first mark.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Why do producers capture only a small percentage of the light that falls on them?
options: Some light is reflected or misses the chlorophyll
Plants do not need much light
Light is used up by respiration
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Light is reflected, passes through, misses the chloroplasts or is the wrong wavelength.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A pyramid of numbers for oak tree → caterpillar → bird is not pyramid-shaped because…
options: one large oak tree feeds many caterpillars
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: A pyramid of numbers ignores size, so one tree gives a narrow bottom bar.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Which pyramid is always pyramid-shaped?
