09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Energy is lost at every transfer, so each level always has less than the one below.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A pyramid of biomass shows…
options: the total dry mass of organisms at each trophic level
the number of organisms at each level
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Biomass is the mass of living material, measured dry.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: When drawing a pyramid of numbers, the school scheme gave marks for…
options: the right shape with the producer at the bottom, and every level labelled
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Shape, producers at the bottom, and labels. Some students forgot to label.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: In grass → rabbit → fox, all the foxes are removed. What happens first?
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: With no predator, more rabbits survive. Later the grass falls and the rabbits may starve.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: In algae → shrimp → fish, the shrimp die. The algae will…
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Fewer shrimp eat the algae, so the algae increase.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: On a predator–prey graph, the predator peak comes…
options: at the same time as the prey peak
only when the prey die out
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Predators respond to more food by breeding, which takes time, so their peak lags behind.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A persistent pesticide is found at the highest concentration in…
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: It is not broken down, and each animal eats many from the level below, so it builds up up the chain.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: An animal in a food web is least affected when one of its prey species declines if it…
options: is at the top of the chain
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: It can switch to eating more of its other prey.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: A blackbird eats earthworms and also eats centipedes that eat woodlice. The blackbird is…
options: both a secondary and a tertiary consumer
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: In a web one animal can feed at more than one trophic level.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: To compare the population of a plant in two fields, a student should…
options: use more quadrats in the field with more plants
sample each field in the same way and compare the means
place quadrats only where plants grow
count one quadrat in each field
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Same quadrat size, same number, random placement in both fields — then compare.

09-ecology-and-the-environment.q: Which is the correct formula for estimating a population with quadrats?
options: total area × area of one quadrat
mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ area of one quadrat)
09-ecology-and-the-environment.explain: Find how many quadrat-sized areas fit in the field, then multiply by the mean count.

10-food-production.q: How does a glasshouse increase crop yield?
options: It removes factors that limit photosynthesis
It adds mineral ions to the soil
10-food-production.explain: It controls temperature, CO₂, light and water, so these stop limiting photosynthesis.

10-food-production.q: Burning a paraffin heater in a glasshouse increases yield because it releases…
10-food-production.explain: Heat raises the temperature and CO₂ is a raw material — two limiting factors removed at once.

10-food-production.q: Why does adding carbon dioxide increase yield?
options: It is a raw material for photosynthesis, so more glucose is made
10-food-production.explain: More CO₂ means more photosynthesis while CO₂ is limiting, so more glucose for growth.

10-food-production.q: A grower adds more and more carbon dioxide. Eventually yield stops rising because…
options: another factor such as light is now limiting
10-food-production.explain: Once CO₂ is no longer limiting, light or temperature limits the rate.

10-food-production.q: Raising a glasshouse from 25 °C to 45 °C reduces yield because…
10-food-production.explain: Above the optimum the enzymes' active sites change shape and the rate falls.

10-food-production.q: Why is nitrate fertiliser added to crops?
options: To make amino acids and proteins for growth
10-food-production.explain: Nitrate ions are needed to make amino acids, which build proteins.

10-food-production.q: Which ion is needed to make chlorophyll?
10-food-production.explain: Magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule.

10-food-production.q: Why do fields need fertiliser when crops are harvested year after year?
options: Mineral ions are removed with the crop and not returned
10-food-production.explain: The crop takes the ions away, so the soil becomes depleted.

10-food-production.q: In a glasshouse investigation into CO₂ concentration, what should be measured?
options: The mass of crop produced after a set time
10-food-production.explain: Yield is the dependent variable — mass of fruit or seeds after a stated time.

10-food-production.q: In the same investigation, which is a control variable?
10-food-production.explain: Temperature must be kept the same. CO₂ is the independent variable; mass of crop is measured.

10-food-production.q: Biological control means…
options: introducing a natural predator of the pest
10-food-production.explain: A natural predator or parasite reduces the pest population.

10-food-production.q: Which is an advantage of biological control over pesticides?
options: It is specific to the pest
10-food-production.explain: This was a real Edexcel question: the only correct answer was that it is specific.

10-food-production.q: Which is a disadvantage of biological control?
options: It is slow to take effect
10-food-production.explain: The other three are problems with pesticides.

10-food-production.q: Why does biological control never wipe out a pest completely?
options: The predator is killed by the pest
The predator needs some pests left as food
10-food-production.explain: If the pest disappeared, the predator would starve. The two settle at a low, steady level.

10-food-production.q: Which is an advantage of pesticides?
10-food-production.explain: Pesticides are fast, but they can kill useful species, build up in food chains and select for resistance.

10-food-production.q: Why do pesticides reach high concentrations in top predators?
options: The pesticide builds up at each trophic level
10-food-production.explain: It is not broken down or excreted, and each animal eats many from the level below.

10-food-production.q: Pests become resistant to a pesticide because…
options: resistant individuals survive, reproduce and pass on the allele
10-food-production.explain: This is natural selection. A mutation gives resistance; survivors pass on the allele.

10-food-production.q: In a pest trial, why is one plot left untreated?
options: As a control to compare with the treatments
10-food-production.explain: The untreated plot shows what happens without any control, so the treatments can be compared with it.

10-food-production.q: Fire ants treated with pesticide recover after six months, but those controlled with phorid flies stay low. This suggests…
10-food-production.explain: The flies keep reproducing, so control continues; the pesticide wears off or resistance develops.

10-food-production.q: Aphids feed from the phloem. Which substance do they mainly take?
10-food-production.explain: Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids. Starch is stored, not transported.

10-food-production.q: Which bacterium is used to make yoghurt?
10-food-production.explain: Lactobacillus converts lactose into lactic acid. Yeast is a fungus used in bread and brewing.

10-food-production.q: Why is milk pasteurised before making yoghurt?
10-food-production.explain: Heating kills other microbes that would compete with Lactobacillus or spoil the yoghurt.

10-food-production.q: Lactobacillus converts…
10-food-production.explain: The sugar in milk is lactose. Anaerobic respiration turns it into lactic acid.

10-food-production.q: What type of respiration does Lactobacillus carry out when making yoghurt?
10-food-production.explain: Lactic acid is a product of anaerobic respiration.

10-food-production.q: Why does milk thicken when it becomes yoghurt?
options: The low pH makes the milk proteins coagulate
10-food-production.explain: Lactic acid lowers the pH, and the proteins clump together.

10-food-production.q: Why does yoghurt keep longer than milk?
options: Its low pH stops other microorganisms growing
10-food-production.explain: The acid acts as a preservative.

10-food-production.q: Yoghurt is made with reduced oxygen. The acidity rises…
options: more slowly, because less respiration happens
faster, because there is more anaerobic respiration
10-food-production.explain: Less oxygen means more anaerobic respiration, so lactic acid is made faster.

10-food-production.q: Why are aseptic precautions used in an industrial fermenter?
options: To prevent contamination by unwanted microorganisms
10-food-production.explain: Other microbes would compete for nutrients and could spoil the product.

10-food-production.q: Why does a fermenter have a cooling water jacket?
options: Respiration releases heat, which would denature enzymes
To add water to the culture
10-food-production.explain: Billions of respiring microbes release a lot of heat, so it must be removed to keep the optimum.

10-food-production.q: Why is air bubbled into a fermenter?
options: To supply oxygen for aerobic respiration
10-food-production.explain: Aerobic respiration releases more energy, so the microorganisms grow faster.

10-food-production.q: Why is the mixture in a fermenter stirred?
options: To keep microorganisms in contact with nutrients and oxygen, and spread heat
10-food-production.explain: Agitation mixes the contents and prevents hot spots.

10-food-production.q: How is the pH kept at the optimum in a fermenter?
options: A temperature probe and water jacket
A pH probe, with acid or alkali added
10-food-production.explain: The probe monitors pH and acid or alkali is added to correct it.

10-food-production.q: Why are nutrients added to a fermenter?
options: To supply raw materials for growth and respiration
10-food-production.explain: The microorganisms need an energy source such as glucose, and materials to build cells.

10-food-production.q: How is contamination prevented in a fermenter?
options: Raising the temperature during the run
Steam-cleaning before use and filtering the incoming air
10-food-production.explain: Sterile vessel and filtered air keep unwanted microbes out.

10-food-production.q: Why is the fermenter kept at the optimum temperature rather than as hot as possible?
options: Enzymes work fastest at the optimum and denature above it
10-food-production.explain: Below the optimum growth is slow; above it the enzymes denature.

10-food-production.q: Selective breeding of fish for fast growth involves…
options: adding growth hormones to the water
breeding the fastest-growing fish, over many generations
10-food-production.explain: Select the fast growers, breed them, select again from the offspring, and repeat.

10-food-production.q: Why is waste food removed from fish tanks?
options: Decomposers feeding on it would use up oxygen
It makes the water too cold
10-food-production.explain: Decomposing waste means lots of bacterial respiration, which lowers the oxygen level for the fish.

10-food-production.q: Why are fish of different sizes kept apart in a fish farm?
options: So larger fish do not eat smaller ones
10-food-production.explain: This controls predation within and between species.

10-food-production.q: Which statement about polythene tunnels is correct?
options: They trap heat and protect crops more cheaply than a glasshouse
10-food-production.explain: Polytunnels work like cheap glasshouses: they keep in heat and keep off wind and some pests.

10-food-production.q: Which chain correctly explains how a glasshouse raises yield?
options: More respiration → more glucose → more growth
More water → less photosynthesis → more growth
More oxygen → more photosynthesis → more yield
Limiting factor removed → more photosynthesis → more glucose → more growth
10-food-production.explain: Name the limiting factor and follow it through. 'The plants grow better' scores nothing.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which is the only process in the carbon cycle that removes carbon dioxide from the air?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Photosynthesis takes CO₂ in. Every other process in the cycle releases it.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which process releases carbon dioxide when fossil fuels are burned?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Burning is combustion. On a cycle diagram, the arrow from a factory or car to the air is combustion.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which two groups of organisms act as decomposers?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi. Viruses are not decomposers.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: How do decomposers release carbon dioxide into the air?
options: By respiring the products of digestion
By absorbing it from the soil
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Decomposers digest dead matter, absorb the products and respire them. Their respiration releases the CO₂.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: In what form does carbon pass from a plant to a herbivore?
options: Carbon compounds such as starch and protein
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Feeding passes carbon compounds along the food chain. Carbon is only CO₂ when it is in the air.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which organisms in the carbon cycle carry out respiration?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Every living organism respires, including plants and decomposers.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: How do fossil fuels form?
options: Dead matter that does not decay is compressed over millions of years
Decomposers turn dead matter into oil
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: When conditions stop decomposers (no oxygen, acidic, waterlogged), dead matter is not broken down and slowly becomes coal, oil and gas.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which conditions make decomposition fastest?
options: Warm, moist and plenty of oxygen
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Decomposers' enzymes work best when warm, need water, and the decomposers respire aerobically.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Why do leaves decompose very slowly in a waterlogged peat bog?
options: There is too much carbon dioxide
There is little oxygen and it is acidic
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Little oxygen and a low pH stop most decomposers, so dead matter builds up.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: A student measures the rate of decomposition of leaves. Which is a suitable measurement?
options: The loss in mass after a set time
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Loss in mass (or CO₂ released) over a stated time measures how fast decomposition happens.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Why can plants not use nitrogen gas from the air directly?
options: There is too little nitrogen in the air
Nitrogen gas is toxic to plants
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: N₂ is very unreactive. Plants take in nitrogen as nitrate ions from the soil.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: In what form do plants absorb most of their nitrogen?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Root hair cells absorb nitrate ions from the soil.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: How do root hair cells absorb nitrate ions from the soil?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Nitrate is usually more concentrated inside the root, so it must be moved against the gradient by active transport.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: What do plants use nitrate for?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Nitrogen is needed for amino acids, and so proteins. Glucose, starch and cellulose contain no nitrogen.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which bacteria convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Nitrogen fixation turns N₂ into compounds plants can use.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Where are nitrogen-fixing bacteria found?
options: In root nodules of legumes and in the soil
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Legumes such as peas, beans and clover have root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which bacteria convert ammonium into nitrate?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Nitrifying bacteria carry out nitrification: ammonium → nitrite → nitrate.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: What is the correct order in nitrification?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Nitrifying bacteria turn ammonium into nitrite, then nitrite into nitrate.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which bacteria convert nitrate into nitrogen gas?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Denitrification returns nitrogen to the air as N₂.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: What do decomposers produce from proteins in dead organisms?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Decomposers break proteins and urea down into ammonium. Nitrifying bacteria then make nitrate.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which statement about nitrifying bacteria is correct?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Nitrifying bacteria are aerobic. That is why waterlogged soil makes less nitrate.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Why does waterlogged soil contain less nitrate?
options: Water dissolves the nitrate into the air
Plants absorb more nitrate when wet
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are killed by water
Denitrifying bacteria thrive without oxygen and nitrifying bacteria stop
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: No oxygen: nitrifying bacteria stop making nitrate, and anaerobic denitrifying bacteria turn nitrate into N₂.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Why does a farmer plough a compacted field?
options: To add oxygen to the soil for nitrifying bacteria
To remove nitrate from the soil
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Air in the soil helps nitrifying bacteria and hinders the anaerobic denitrifying bacteria.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Why do farmers grow clover and then plough it into the soil?
options: Clover absorbs nitrate from the soil
Clover's root nodules add nitrogen compounds to the soil
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Clover is a legume. Its nitrogen-fixing bacteria add nitrogen compounds, which end up as nitrate.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: What do legume plants give to the bacteria in their root nodules?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: The plant supplies sugars; the bacteria supply nitrogen compounds. Both benefit.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: A fish farm filter contains bacteria that remove ammonium from the water. What type are they?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Nitrifying bacteria convert toxic ammonium into nitrite and then nitrate.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which of these is NOT a stage of the carbon cycle named in the specification?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Nitrification belongs to the nitrogen cycle. The carbon cycle stages are photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: On a carbon-cycle diagram, an arrow goes from carbon dioxide in the air to green plants. What process is it?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Only photosynthesis moves carbon from the air into plants.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: On a carbon-cycle diagram, an arrow goes from animals to carbon dioxide in the air. What process is it?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Animals return CO₂ to the air by respiration.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Plants store carbon in a compound that decays very slowly. Why does this reduce carbon dioxide in the air?
options: Less carbon dioxide is released by the respiration of decomposers
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: If decomposers break the compound down slowly, the carbon stays locked away instead of being respired back as CO₂.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Animals get the nitrogen they need by:
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Animals digest proteins to amino acids and build their own proteins.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which nitrogen compound do mammals excrete in urine, which decomposers later convert to ammonium?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Urea is broken down by decomposers into ammonium.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: A crop in waterlogged soil has yellow leaves and grows slowly. What is the most likely cause?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Waterlogging reduces soil nitrate, so the plant cannot make enough amino acids and proteins.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which process adds carbon to the air that was stored for millions of years?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Burning coal, oil and gas releases ancient carbon very quickly.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: How do decomposers digest dead matter?
options: They secrete enzymes onto it and absorb the products
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Bacteria and fungi digest outside their cells, then absorb the small soluble molecules.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: An examiner writes 'Ignore breakdown'. Which answer about leaf litter would score?
options: The leaves are decomposed by bacteria and fungi
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Name the process (decomposition) and the organisms (bacteria and fungi).

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Which change would increase the nitrate content of soil?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Decomposers and nitrifying bacteria turn the proteins in manure into nitrate.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: What happens to the nitrogen gas released by denitrifying bacteria?
options: It forms proteins in the soil
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Denitrification returns nitrogen to the air, completing the cycle.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: Why is deforestation linked to rising carbon dioxide in two ways?
options: Less photosynthesis, and the trees are burned or decompose
More nitrogen fixation and less decomposition
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Fewer trees remove less CO₂, and their stored carbon is released.

11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.q: In the nitrogen cycle, which pair of organisms has opposite effects on soil nitrate?
11-carbon-and-nitrogen-cycles.explain: Nitrifying bacteria make nitrate; denitrifying bacteria remove it as nitrogen gas.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which gas dissolves in rain to form acid rain?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Sulfur dioxide from burning fossil fuels dissolves in water to make acid rain.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: What is the main source of sulfur dioxide pollution?
options: Burning fossil fuels that contain sulfur
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Coal and oil contain sulfur. Volcanoes are a natural source.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which is a biological consequence of acid rain?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Acid rain lowers the pH of lakes, killing fish and other aquatic organisms. It also damages trees.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Carbon monoxide is produced by:
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: When fuel burns with too little oxygen, carbon monoxide forms.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous?
options: It binds to haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen
It dissolves in water to form an acid
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin and does not let go, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which of these is NOT a greenhouse gas?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Carbon monoxide is a pollutant, not a greenhouse gas. Edexcel rejects it.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which gases are all greenhouse gases?
options: Sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: The spec's five are CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs and water vapour.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which is a major source of methane?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Cattle digestion, rice paddy fields and landfill release methane.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which human activity releases nitrous oxide?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Soil bacteria convert fertiliser nitrogen, releasing nitrous oxide. Vehicle engines release some too.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: How do greenhouse gases warm the Earth?
options: They reflect sunlight back into space
They absorb infrared radiation from the Earth and re-radiate it
They make a hole in the ozone layer
They produce heat by reacting with oxygen
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Greenhouse gases absorb the infrared given off by the warm Earth, trapping heat.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: What is the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: The natural warming of the Earth
Extra warming caused by increased greenhouse gases from human activity
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: The natural greenhouse effect is necessary. The enhanced effect comes from the extra gases humans add.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which is a biological consequence of global warming?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Habitat change forces migration or extinction. Other accepted answers: habitat loss from flooding, coral bleaching.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Why does global warming cause flooding of low-lying habitats?
options: Ice caps melt and sea levels rise
More sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Melting ice and warmer water raise sea levels.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth would be:
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Emissions from four sources are 50, 110, 118 and 175 million tonnes. What percentage comes from the 110 source?
A forest shrinks from 41 200 km² to 40 000 km² in 25 years. What is the mean rate of loss?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: 1200 ÷ 25 = 48 km² per year.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: What is eutrophication?
options: Excess nutrients in water causing algal growth and oxygen depletion
Loss of trees from a forest
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Nitrate and phosphate cause an algal bloom, and decomposition then uses up the oxygen.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which ions from fertilisers cause eutrophication?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Nitrate and phosphate leached from farmland feed the algae.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: In eutrophication, why do plants at the bottom of a lake die?
options: The algal bloom blocks the light
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Algae on the surface block light, so plants below cannot photosynthesise.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: In eutrophication, what uses up most of the oxygen in the water?
options: Bacteria decomposing dead plants and algae
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: The huge bacterial population respires aerobically and strips the dissolved oxygen.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Put the eutrophication steps in order: P plants die; Q algae grow; R bacteria respire; S nitrate enters the lake.
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Nitrate enters, algae grow and block light, plants die, bacteria decompose them and respire.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Why do fish die at the end of eutrophication?
options: There is too little oxygen for respiration
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Bacterial respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen, so fish cannot respire.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: How can untreated sewage kill fish even without an algal bloom?
options: Bacteria feeding on it respire and use up oxygen
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Sewage is organic matter — food for bacteria, whose respiration removes the oxygen.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: An examiner writes 'Ignore nutrients'. Which answer would score for eutrophication?
options: Nitrate from fertiliser is leached into the river
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Name the ion (nitrate or phosphate) and the route (leaching or run-off).

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Oxygen levels in a eutrophic lake are high while algae are alive. Why?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Living algae release oxygen by photosynthesis. The crash comes after they die and are decomposed.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Crabs in a fish farm eat waste food and faeces. How does this reduce pollution?
options: Less decomposition, so less bacterial respiration and more oxygen
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Less waste means fewer decomposing bacteria, so less oxygen is used up.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Seaweed grown next to a fish farm absorbs nitrate. What is the benefit?
options: Less algal growth, so less eutrophication
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Removing nitrate starves the algae, preventing a bloom.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: What is leaching?
options: Soil being blown away by wind
Minerals being washed out of the soil by rain
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Rain washes dissolved mineral ions down and out of the soil.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Why does deforestation cause soil erosion?
options: No roots hold the soil, so rain washes it away
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Tree roots bind soil and the canopy breaks the force of the rain.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: How does deforestation reduce local rainfall?
options: Less transpiration, so less water vapour in the air
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Trees release huge amounts of water vapour by transpiration (evapotranspiration).

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Deforestation increases carbon dioxide in the air because:
options: Less photosynthesis, and the trees are burned or decompose
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Two effects: less CO₂ removed, and stored carbon released.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which is an effect of deforestation on biodiversity?
options: It increases the number of species
It creates new habitats in the canopy
Habitats are destroyed, so species are lost
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Removing trees removes food and shelter for many species.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: After deforestation, minerals wash into a river. Which use of a mineral is correctly matched?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Magnesium is needed for chlorophyll; nitrate for amino acids and proteins.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: A town switches from coal to biogas. Which is a possible drawback?
options: More sulfur dioxide, causing acid rain
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: The Year 11 mock accepted more sulfur dioxide and acid rain as a drawback.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: A pregnant woman smokes. Why may her baby have a low birth mass?
options: Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen carried to the fetus
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Less oxygen reaches the fetus, so less respiration and slower growth.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which of these is an old source of CFCs?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: CFCs were used in fridges and aerosol cans. They are now banned.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which answer about global warming would score a consequence mark?
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: A consequence must be a result, like coral bleaching or habitat loss — not the warming itself.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Why can burning trees be worse for CO₂ levels than burning the same mass of fossil fuel over time?
options: Removing trees also stops future photosynthesis
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Deforestation both releases carbon and removes a plant that would have kept absorbing CO₂.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which statement about the ozone layer is correct for this topic?
options: Greenhouse gases make a hole in it
Ozone depletion is a different problem from the greenhouse effect
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Do not confuse the two. The greenhouse effect is about trapping infrared.

12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.q: Which change would most reduce eutrophication of a river next to farmland?
options: Adding more fertiliser before heavy rain
Draining the fields into the river
Cutting down trees along the bank
Planting strips of vegetation along the bank
12-human-impacts-on-the-environment.explain: Plants along the bank absorb nitrate before it reaches the water.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Body cells are diploid: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: How many chromosomes are in a human gamete?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Gametes are haploid: one chromosome from each pair, 23 in total.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: What does diploid mean?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Diploid cells have two sets — one from each parent.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Mitosis produces:
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Mitosis: two, identical, diploid.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Meiosis produces:
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Meiosis: four, different, haploid gametes.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Where does meiosis take place in humans?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Meiosis only happens in the sex organs, to make gametes.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which process is NOT a use of mitosis?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Gametes are made by meiosis. Mitosis is for growth, repair, cloning and asexual reproduction.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: What happens to each chromosome just before a cell divides?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Each chromosome is copied, which is why it looks like an X before division.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Why must gametes be haploid?
options: So fertilisation restores the diploid number
So they can divide by mitosis
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: 23 + 23 = 46. Diploid gametes would double the number every generation.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which two things produce genetic variation in sexual reproduction?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Meiosis makes every gamete different; random fertilisation combines them by chance.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: What is fertilisation?
options: Release of an egg from the ovary
Transfer of sperm into the vagina
Fusion of a male and female gamete nucleus
Embedding of the embryo in the uterus
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Fertilisation is the fusion of the nuclei, making a zygote.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: What is a zygote?
options: The diploid cell formed at fertilisation
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: The zygote then divides by mitosis to form an embryo.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Where does fertilisation normally take place?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Sperm meet the egg in the oviduct. The embryo implants later in the uterus.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Why can a red blood cell not be used to show a karyotype?
options: It has no nucleus, so no chromosomes
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which type of cell division produces white blood cells?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Body cells, including white blood cells, are made by mitosis.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: How can you tell from a karyotype that a person is male?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Males are XY; females are XX.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: A karyotype shows 45 chromosomes with a single X. What is the likely cause?
options: Sex chromosomes failed to separate during meiosis
A mutation in a white blood cell
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: One gamete lacked a sex chromosome because the pair did not separate properly in meiosis.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: A person has 45 chromosomes with a single X and no Y. Which is correct?
options: The person is female, with less oestrogen and usually infertile
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: No Y means female. The ovaries do not develop normally, so less oestrogen and usually no eggs.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which structure makes sperm?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: The testes make sperm by meiosis, and testosterone.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: What is the job of the glands such as the prostate?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: The fluid carries nutrients and lets sperm swim.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which structure carries sperm from the testes towards the urethra?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: The sperm duct links the testes to the urethra.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Where does an embryo implant?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: The embryo embeds in the thick lining of the uterus.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which hormone causes the secondary sexual characteristics in boys?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Testosterone from the testes: deeper voice, facial hair, muscles, sperm production.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which is a secondary sexual characteristic caused by oestrogen?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Oestrogen causes breast development, wider hips and the start of the menstrual cycle.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which gland produces FSH and LH?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: FSH and LH come from the pituitary. Oestrogen and progesterone come from the ovary.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: What does FSH do?
options: Causes an egg to mature in the ovary
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: FSH matures an egg (follicle) and stimulates oestrogen release.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which hormone triggers ovulation?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: A surge of LH causes the egg to be released, at about day 14.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which hormone builds up the uterus lining?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Oestrogen builds the lining; progesterone maintains it.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which hormone maintains the uterus lining and inhibits FSH and LH?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Progesterone keeps the lining ready for an embryo and stops new eggs maturing.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: What happens if the egg is not fertilised?
options: Progesterone rises and the lining thickens
Progesterone falls and the lining breaks down
LH rises and a second egg is released at once
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Falling progesterone means the lining is no longer maintained — menstruation.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Around which day of a 28-day cycle does ovulation usually happen?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Ovulation is around the middle of the cycle, about day 14.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Why do contraceptive tablets containing progesterone prevent pregnancy?
options: They inhibit FSH and LH, so no egg matures or is released
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Progesterone stops FSH and LH, so there is no egg to fertilise.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which is a disadvantage of a daily contraceptive tablet compared with an implant?
options: It is easy to forget to take
It needs a doctor to fit it
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Tablets must be taken every day. Implants need no daily action.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which substance passes from the mother to the fetus across the placenta?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Glucose, amino acids and oxygen pass to the fetus. The bloods never mix, so red cells do not cross.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which substance passes from the fetus to the mother?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Urea and carbon dioxide are waste products removed through the placenta.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: How do substances cross the placenta?
options: Through the umbilical vein into the mother
By diffusion across a thin barrier
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Diffusion (and some active transport) across a thin, large-surface-area barrier. The bloods do not mix.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: What is the job of the amniotic fluid?
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Amniotic fluid cushions the fetus against physical damage.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Which is a difference between sexual and asexual reproduction?
options: Sexual reproduction produces varied offspring; asexual produces clones
Sexual reproduction needs only one parent
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Sexual reproduction mixes genes from two parents; asexual uses mitosis from one.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: What is the advantage of variation from sexual reproduction?
options: Offspring are identical to the parent
A species is more likely to survive environmental change or disease
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Some varied individuals may survive a new disease or changed conditions.

13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.q: Why is the chance of having a boy 50%?
options: Eggs carry X or Y equally
Half of all sperm carry X and half carry Y
13-cell-division-and-human-reproduction.explain: Meiosis in an XY male gives equal numbers of X and Y sperm; every egg carries X.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: The anther makes pollen. Anther + filament = stamen.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: What is pollination?
options: Transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
Fusion of male and female nuclei
Growth of a seed into a plant
Release of seeds from a fruit
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Pollination is the transfer. Fertilisation is the later fusion.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: On which structure do pollen grains germinate?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: The pollen grain germinates on the stigma and grows a tube down the style.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Through which structure does the pollen tube grow?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: The pollen tube grows down the style to the ovary.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which structure becomes the seed?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: The fertilised ovule becomes the seed.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which structure becomes the fruit?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: The ovary develops into the fruit, containing the seeds.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: What is fertilisation in a flowering plant?
options: Fusion of the male nucleus with the female nucleus in the ovule
Release of pollen from the anther
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Fertilisation is the fusion of the nuclei inside the ovule.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which is the correct order of events?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Pollen lands, the tube grows down the style, then the nuclei fuse.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which feature is typical of an insect-pollinated flower?
options: Anthers hanging outside on long filaments
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Bright petals attract insects. The other three are wind-pollination features.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which feature is typical of a wind-pollinated flower?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: A large, feathery, exposed stigma catches pollen from the air.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why do wind-pollinated flowers produce huge amounts of pollen?
options: Most pollen is lost, so lots is needed for some to reach a stigma
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Wind carries pollen randomly, so most is wasted.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: What is the pollen of a wind-pollinated flower like?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Light, smooth pollen is carried easily by the wind.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why are the anthers of an insect-pollinated flower inside the flower?
options: So pollen rubs onto the insect as it reaches the nectar
So wind can blow the pollen
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: The insect brushes past the anthers on its way to the nectary.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: What is the job of the nectary?
options: To make sugary nectar that attracts insects
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Nectar is the insect's reward for visiting.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why are the filaments of a wind-pollinated flower long?
options: So the anthers hang outside and shake in the wind
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Long, loose filaments expose the anthers to the wind.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: What is cross-pollination?
options: Pollen moving to a stigma on the same flower
Pollen moving from stigma to anther
Pollen moving between flowers on different plants of the same species
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Cross-pollination involves two plants, so gametes with different alleles fuse.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why does cross-pollination give more variation than self-pollination?
options: Gametes from two different plants with different alleles fuse
It happens only in wind-pollinated flowers
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Two parents contribute different alleles.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which three conditions do seeds need to germinate?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Not light.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why is water needed for germination?
options: To activate enzymes that break down the food store
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Water makes the seed swell and activates its enzymes.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why is oxygen needed for germination?
options: To make the seed coat split
For aerobic respiration, releasing energy for growth
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Germinating seeds respire aerobically to release energy.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why is a suitable temperature needed for germination?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Too cold and enzymes work very slowly; too hot and they denature.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why is light NOT needed for germination?
options: The seed uses its stored food until its leaves can photosynthesise
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: The mock scheme rejected 'light for photosynthesis' — seeds do not photosynthesise yet.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: In the germination practical, why is water boiled before adding the seeds?
options: To kill bacteria on the seeds
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Boiling drives out dissolved oxygen, so the tube tests whether oxygen is needed.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why is a layer of oil added on top of the boiled, cooled water?
options: To stop light reaching the seeds
To stop oxygen dissolving back in
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: The oil seals the water from the air.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which tube in a germination experiment is the control?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: The control has all three conditions, so it shows what happens when nothing is missing.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Seeds on dry cotton wool at 20 °C do not germinate. Which condition is missing?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Dry cotton wool tests for water.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which enzyme digests the starch stored in a germinating seed?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Amylase breaks starch down into sugars for respiration and growth.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why does the dry mass of a seedling fall during the first few days?
options: It respires stored food, releasing carbon dioxide
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Respiration turns stored starch into CO₂, which is lost.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why does the dry mass of a seedling later increase?
options: Its leaves photosynthesise faster than it respires
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Once leaves open, photosynthesis makes more glucose than respiration uses.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which is a natural method of asexual reproduction in plants?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Strawberry runners grow along the ground and root to form clones.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which is an artificial method of asexual reproduction accepted by Edexcel in 2024?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Cuttings. The 2024 scheme rejected tissue culture for that part.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why are plants grown from runners genetically identical to the parent?
options: They are made by mitosis with no fusion of gametes
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Asexual reproduction uses mitosis, so the offspring are clones.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why are the lower leaves removed from a cutting?
options: To reduce water loss by transpiration
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: With no roots yet, the cutting must not lose too much water.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: What is an advantage of producing plants by cuttings?
options: The offspring show lots of variation
All the offspring have the parent's desired characteristics
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Clones keep the colour, flavour or yield that the grower wants.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: What is a disadvantage of a crop made entirely of clones?
options: One disease could kill them all because there is no variation
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Genetically identical plants share the same weaknesses.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: How do animals disperse the seeds in fleshy fruits?
options: They carry them on their feet only
They eat the fruit and egest the seeds elsewhere
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Seeds survive the gut and are deposited in faeces far from the parent.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Why is it an advantage for seeds to land far from the parent plant?
options: Less competition for light, water and mineral ions
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Seedlings near the parent would compete with it for resources.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: A pea pod contains six peas. How many ovules were fertilised?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Each pea is a seed from one fertilised ovule. The pod is the fruit from one ovary.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: A student counts insect visits to flowers of different colours. Which variable should be kept the same?
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: Scent could also attract insects, so it must be controlled. Colour is the independent variable.

14-reproduction-in-plants.q: Which statement about pollination and fertilisation is correct?
options: A flower can be pollinated without being fertilised
14-reproduction-in-plants.explain: If no pollen tube reaches the ovule, pollination happens but fertilisation does not.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is the genome of an organism?
options: All the DNA of the organism
The genes that code for enzymes
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The genome is the entire DNA of an organism — every chromosome, every gene.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is a gene?
options: A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein
A different version of an allele
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A gene is a section of a DNA molecule that codes for one specific protein.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where in a human cell are the chromosomes found?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Chromosomes are in the nucleus, and genes are located on them.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which describes the structure of a DNA molecule?
options: One strand folded into a ball
Two strands coiled into a double helix
A single strand in a ring
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: DNA is two strands coiled to form a double helix, linked by paired bases.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which base pairs with adenine (A) in DNA?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: In DNA, A pairs with T and C pairs with G. Uracil is only found in RNA.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which base pairs with cytosine (C)?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: C always pairs with G.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What are the three parts of a nucleotide?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Each nucleotide is a sugar, a phosphate group and one of four bases.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: One strand of DNA reads TAC CGT. What is the complementary DNA strand?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Swap each base for its partner: T→A, A→T, C→G, G→C. DNA never contains U.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: RNA contains uracil (U) instead of thymine (T).

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which is a correct difference between DNA and RNA?
options: DNA is single-stranded; RNA is double-stranded
DNA contains ribose; RNA contains deoxyribose
DNA contains thymine; RNA contains uracil
DNA is short; RNA is very long
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: DNA: double-stranded, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: single-stranded, ribose, uracil.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where does transcription take place?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Transcription — making mRNA from DNA — happens in the nucleus, where the DNA is.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is made during transcription?
options: A new copy of the chromosome
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Transcription copies the base sequence of a gene into messenger RNA.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is the mRNA made from the DNA strand ATTCCGAGT?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Pair each base (A→U, T→A, C→G, G→C). RNA has U, never T.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where does translation take place?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Translation happens at the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is the job of tRNA in protein synthesis?
options: Carries the code out of the nucleus
Brings specific amino acids to the ribosome
Joins the two strands of DNA
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Each tRNA carries one specific amino acid to the ribosome. mRNA carries the code.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is a codon?
options: Three bases on mRNA that code for one amino acid
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A codon is a triplet of bases on mRNA. The matching triplet on tRNA is the anticodon.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where is the anticodon found?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The anticodon is on tRNA and is complementary to a codon on mRNA.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which is the correct order for protein synthesis?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Transcription copies DNA into RNA; translation turns the RNA code into protein.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: How many bases code for one amino acid?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The code is read in triplets — three bases per amino acid.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: A section of mRNA is 90 bases long. How many amino acids does it code for?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: 90 ÷ 3 = 30. Each codon of three bases codes for one amino acid.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Why is mRNA needed to make proteins?
options: Amino acids are only found in the nucleus
DNA stays in the nucleus but proteins are made at ribosomes in the cytoplasm
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: mRNA is a mobile copy of the gene that carries the code from the nucleus to the ribosomes.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: During translation, what joins to the mRNA codon?
options: The anticodon of a tRNA molecule
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A tRNA with a complementary anticodon binds to the codon and delivers its amino acid.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What happens to the amino acids brought to the ribosome?
options: They are joined into a chain — a polypeptide
They are broken down for energy
They are stored in the nucleus
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The amino acids are joined in the order set by the codons, forming a polypeptide that folds into a protein.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What decides the shape of a protein?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The order of amino acids decides how the chain folds, and so the protein's shape.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: What is a mutation?
options: A rare, random change in the base sequence of DNA
A change in the number of ribosomes
A new combination of alleles at fertilisation
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A mutation is a rare, random change in genetic material, which can be inherited.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: A mutation changes one codon so that a different amino acid is added. What is the most likely result for an enzyme?
options: The active site may change shape so the substrate no longer fits
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A different amino acid can change the folding and so the shape of the active site.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which statement about mutations is correct?
options: Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Most mutations have no effect, some have a small effect, and only rarely is the effect significant.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Why might a change in one base have no effect on the protein?
options: The new codon may code for the same amino acid
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Many amino acids have more than one codon, so the amino acid — and the protein — can stay the same.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: A person has one mutated allele of a gene but no symptoms. What is the most likely reason?
options: The mutation is in a ribosome
The mutation made the gene longer
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A recessive allele is not expressed while a dominant, working allele is present.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which of these increases the rate of mutation?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Ionising radiation — gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet — increases the incidence of mutations.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which is a chemical mutagen?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Some chemicals, such as those in tobacco, increase the rate of mutation.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which type of radiation is NOT ionising?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Gamma, X-rays and UV are ionising and can cause mutations. Radio waves are not.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Where do new alleles come from?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Mutation is the only source of brand-new alleles. Meiosis and fertilisation shuffle existing ones.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: An amino acid has 4 codons, a second has 2 and a third has 1. How many mRNA sequences could code for all three in that order?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Multiply the choices: 4 × 2 × 1 = 8.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which structure is the site of protein synthesis?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Proteins are assembled at ribosomes during translation.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: During transcription, which base in the mRNA pairs with adenine on the DNA?
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: RNA has no thymine, so uracil pairs with adenine.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Which row is correct for translation?
options: Codon on tRNA, anticodon on mRNA
Codon on mRNA, anticodon on tRNA
Codon on DNA, anticodon on mRNA
Codon on tRNA, anticodon on DNA
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: The codon is on mRNA; the complementary anticodon is on tRNA.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: How does a gene affect a characteristic such as eye colour?
options: The gene itself is the colour
The gene moves to the eye
The gene is made of pigment
It codes for a protein, which affects the characteristic
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: A gene codes for a protein — often an enzyme — and the protein produces the characteristic.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Beta thalassaemia is caused by a mutation in a haemoglobin gene. Why do people with it tire quickly?
options: Less haemoglobin means less oxygen carried, so less respiration in muscles
Their lungs cannot take in air
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Less working haemoglobin carries less oxygen, so less aerobic respiration and less energy released.

15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.q: Near a radioactive leak, more abnormal butterflies are found. Why can't scientists be certain the radiation caused them?
options: There is no control group or data from before the leak
15-dna-and-protein-synthesis.explain: Without a control or earlier data, the normal level of abnormality is unknown, and other factors could be responsible.

16-inheritance.q: What is an allele?
options: A different form of the same gene
16-inheritance.explain: Alleles are alternative versions of a gene, which cause differences in inherited characteristics.

16-inheritance.q: What is meant by a dominant allele?
options: It is the most common allele
It is stronger than other alleles
It is only expressed with two copies
Only one copy is needed for it to be expressed in the phenotype
16-inheritance.explain: A dominant allele is expressed even when only one copy is present. It is not necessarily common.

16-inheritance.q: What is meant by a recessive allele?
options: Only expressed when two copies are present
16-inheritance.explain: A recessive allele is only expressed when no dominant allele is present — two copies.

16-inheritance.q: Which genotype is heterozygous?
16-inheritance.explain: Heterozygous means two different alleles.

16-inheritance.q: Which genotype is homozygous recessive?
16-inheritance.explain: Homozygous recessive means two identical recessive alleles.

16-inheritance.q: What is the phenotype of an organism?
16-inheritance.explain: Phenotype is what you can observe; genotype is the combination of alleles.

16-inheritance.q: Which is a genotype?
16-inheritance.explain: Genotypes are written as alleles. The others are phenotypes.

16-inheritance.q: An organism shows the recessive characteristic. What is its genotype?
16-inheritance.explain: A recessive phenotype can only come from two recessive alleles.

16-inheritance.q: An organism shows the dominant characteristic. What could its genotype be?
16-inheritance.explain: BB and Bb look the same, because one dominant allele is enough.

16-inheritance.q: How many alleles of each gene does a gamete carry?
16-inheritance.explain: Gametes are made by meiosis and carry one chromosome of each pair, so one allele of each gene.

16-inheritance.q: What gametes can a parent with genotype Hh produce?
16-inheritance.explain: Each gamete gets one allele, so half carry H and half carry h.

16-inheritance.q: Hh is crossed with hh. What is the expected ratio of offspring phenotypes?
16-inheritance.explain: The offspring are Hh, Hh, hh, hh — half show the dominant characteristic.

16-inheritance.q: Two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) are crossed. What is the expected ratio of phenotypes?
16-inheritance.explain: AA, Aa, Aa, aa: three show the dominant characteristic, one the recessive. 1 : 2 : 1 is the genotype ratio.

16-inheritance.q: Two parents are Aa × Aa. What is the probability of an aa child?
16-inheritance.explain: One of the four equally likely outcomes is aa: 1/4 = 0.25.

16-inheritance.q: Two parents are Aa × Aa. What is the probability of a heterozygous child?
16-inheritance.explain: Two of the four boxes are Aa: 2/4 = 0.5.

16-inheritance.q: AA is crossed with aa. What are the offspring?
16-inheritance.explain: One parent can only give A and the other only a, so every offspring is Aa.

16-inheritance.q: Black rats are crossed with agouti rats and all the offspring are agouti. What does this show?
16-inheritance.explain: The offspring carry both alleles but only agouti shows, so agouti is dominant.

16-inheritance.q: Two unaffected parents have a child with a genetic condition. What does this show?
options: The condition is recessive and both parents are carriers
Only the mother carries the allele
The child has a new mutation in every cell
16-inheritance.explain: The child must be homozygous recessive, so each unaffected parent must be heterozygous.

16-inheritance.q: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. Two carriers have a child. What is the chance the child has cystic fibrosis?
16-inheritance.explain: Ff × Ff gives 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff, so 1 in 4.

16-inheritance.q: Two carriers already have one child with cystic fibrosis. What is the chance their next child has it?
16-inheritance.explain: Each fertilisation is independent. The chance stays 1 in 4 for every child.

16-inheritance.q: What is the probability of a child being male?
16-inheritance.explain: Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y; eggs all carry X.

16-inheritance.q: What are the sex chromosomes of a human male?
16-inheritance.explain: Females are XX and males are XY.

16-inheritance.q: Which gamete decides the sex of a child?
16-inheritance.explain: Every egg carries X. A sperm carries X or Y, so the sperm decides.

16-inheritance.q: Aa × Aa, where A is dominant. What is the probability of a child that is male AND shows the dominant characteristic?
16-inheritance.explain: Multiply: P(male) × P(dominant) = 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8 = 0.375.

16-inheritance.q: Two roan cattle (CRCW) are mated. What is the probability of a male roan calf?
Two parents are Ff × Ff. What is the probability that their next two children both have the recessive condition?
16-inheritance.explain: Each child independently has a 1/4 chance: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

16-inheritance.q: What does codominance mean?
options: The alleles are on different chromosomes
Both alleles are expressed in the phenotype
16-inheritance.explain: With codominance, the heterozygote shows both alleles — like roan cattle or blood group AB.

16-inheritance.q: Red cattle (CRCR) are crossed with white cattle (CWCW). The alleles are codominant. What are the calves?
16-inheritance.explain: Every calf is CRCW, and with codominance that is roan.

16-inheritance.q: Two roan cattle are mated. What is the expected ratio of calves?
16-inheritance.explain: CRCW × CRCW gives CRCR, CRCW, CRCW, CWCW — red, roan, roan, white.

16-inheritance.q: Parents have blood group genotypes IAIO and IBIO. Which blood groups could their children have?
16-inheritance.explain: The four boxes are IAIB (AB), IAIO (A), IBIO (B) and IOIO (O).

16-inheritance.q: Which person has blood group O?
16-inheritance.explain: IO is recessive, so group O needs two IO alleles.

16-inheritance.q: In a pedigree diagram, what does a shaded circle usually show?
16-inheritance.explain: Circles are females and squares are males; shading shows the condition.

16-inheritance.q: A person with a recessive condition (ff) has a child with an unaffected person. The child is unaffected. What is the child's genotype?
16-inheritance.explain: The child must have received f from the affected parent, but is unaffected, so is Ff.

16-inheritance.q: A cross gives 608 plants with one characteristic and 250 with the other. What is the ratio in the form n : 1?
Why does a cross expected to give 3 : 1 rarely give exactly 3 : 1?
options: Which gametes fuse at fertilisation is random
16-inheritance.explain: A ratio is a probability. Chance decides which gametes meet, so real numbers vary around it.

16-inheritance.q: How could a breeder find out whether a black dog is BB or Bb (black dominant)?
options: Breed it with a brown dog (bb) and look for brown puppies
Breed it with another BB dog
Look at its fur more closely
16-inheritance.explain: Any brown puppy must have received b from the black parent, proving it is Bb.

16-inheritance.q: What is polygenic inheritance?
options: A characteristic controlled by many genes
16-inheritance.explain: Polygenic means many genes. Most characteristics, such as height, are polygenic.

16-inheritance.q: Why is there a wider range of heights in a herd of cattle than hair colours?
options: Hair colour is affected by diet
Height is controlled by one gene
Height is polygenic and also affected by the environment
16-inheritance.explain: Many genes each add a little to height, and nutrition affects it too, so there is a smooth range.

16-inheritance.q: Why is a harmful recessive allele harder for breeders to remove than a dominant one?
options: It is hidden in heterozygous carriers that look normal
16-inheritance.explain: Carriers show no sign, so they are bred from and pass the allele on unnoticed.

16-inheritance.q: How can you tell from a karyotype that a person is male?
options: The 23rd pair is one X and one smaller Y
16-inheritance.explain: Males are XY, so the sex chromosome pair is unmatched — one large X, one small Y.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which of these is an example of variation caused only by the environment?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: A scar comes from an injury during life, not from alleles.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which characteristic is affected by both genes and the environment?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Genes set a range of possible heights; diet and health decide where in it a person ends up.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which is the only source of brand-new alleles?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Meiosis and fertilisation shuffle existing alleles; mutation creates new ones.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which of these does NOT produce genetic variation?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells, so it gives no variation.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Identical twins raised apart differ in body mass. What causes the difference?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Identical twins have identical alleles, so any difference must be environmental.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Whose theory explains evolution by natural selection?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Charles Darwin proposed evolution by natural selection.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is the first step in natural selection?
options: A mutation produces variation in the population
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Variation must exist first — new alleles arise by random mutation.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: In natural selection, what is passed on to the offspring?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: The mark scheme wants alleles or genes. 'Passes on the mutation' or 'behaviour' alone did not score.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which is the correct order of natural selection?
options: Variation → survive → reproduce → pass on alleles
Reproduce → variation → pass on alleles → survive
Pass on alleles → survive → variation → reproduce
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Mutation gives variation; the best suited survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why are individuals with an advantageous characteristic more likely to pass on their alleles?
options: They are more likely to survive and reproduce
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Surviving to breed is what lets an allele reach the next generation.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Some woodlice roll into a ball when touched. How does this give a survival advantage?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Rolling up exposes only the hard outer shell, so they are less likely to be eaten.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which statement about adaptation by natural selection is correct?
options: Individuals change during their lives to suit the environment
The population changes over many generations
Organisms learn new features and pass them on
Features used a lot become inherited
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Individuals do not change; the proportion of alleles in the population changes over generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is evolution?
options: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time
Growth of an organism during its life
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Evolution is a change in inherited characteristics over many generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: When have two populations become separate species?
options: When they live in different places
When they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Separate species cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Giant whales are thought to have replaced the shark megalodon. Which idea best explains this?
options: The whales mutated to become sharks
The whales were better adapted, so they won the competition for food
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Competition for the same food: the better-adapted whales survived and reproduced more.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: How do bacteria first become resistant to an antibiotic?
options: They absorb resistance from the patient
A random mutation produces a resistance allele
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: The resistance allele comes from a random mutation. The antibiotic only selects it.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What does the antibiotic do in the development of resistance?
options: Kills the non-resistant bacteria, leaving resistant ones to multiply
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: It removes the competition, so the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why does antibiotic resistance spread so quickly?
options: Bacteria reproduce very quickly, so there are many generations
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Bacteria can divide every 20 minutes or so, so selection happens over many generations quickly.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is MRSA?
options: A strain of bacteria resistant to many antibiotics
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: MRSA is a strain of Staphylococcus aureus resistant to many antibiotics.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why should antibiotics not be prescribed for a cold?
options: Colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not kill
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Antibiotics do not affect viruses. Using them anyway selects for resistant bacteria.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why are patients told to finish a course of antibiotics?
options: To stop them catching a virus
To kill all the bacteria, including the more resistant ones
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Stopping early can leave the more resistant bacteria alive to multiply.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why are resistant infections difficult to control?
options: The antibiotic no longer kills the bacteria, so they keep spreading
Resistant bacteria cannot be passed between people
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: The usual antibiotic fails, so the bacteria keep multiplying and spreading.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Fire ant numbers fall after pesticide, then rise again. Which explanation uses natural selection?
options: The ants learned to avoid the pesticide
The pesticide caused mutations in all the ants
Resistant ants survived, reproduced and passed on the resistance allele
The ants moved away and came back
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: A few ants already had a resistance allele; they survived and bred.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Who chooses which individuals reproduce in selective breeding?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: In selective breeding, humans pick the parents with the characteristic they want.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which is the correct sequence for selective breeding?
options: Breed any two parents once and keep all offspring
Select parents, breed, select best offspring, repeat over many generations
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: The key words are select, breed, select the offspring, and repeat over many generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which is an example of selective breeding?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: High-yield wheat was produced by humans choosing and crossing the best plants over generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why is dwarf wheat useful to farmers?
options: It is resistant to all diseases
It grows taller and catches more light
Less energy goes into the stem, so more into grain, and it is less likely to fall over
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: A short, thick stem means more energy for grain and less damage from wind and rain.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Which characteristic might a farmer selectively breed for in dairy cows?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Dairy farmers select cows that give the most milk.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is the main disadvantage of selective breeding?
options: It is faster than natural selection
It increases the number of alleles
It reduces variation, making the population vulnerable to disease
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Breeding from a few related individuals narrows the range of alleles.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What is inbreeding?
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Inbreeding means breeding related individuals, which increases the chance of genetic disorders.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why does inbreeding increase genetic disorders?
options: Related parents are more likely to carry the same harmful recessive allele
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Two carriers of the same recessive allele are more likely to meet, producing homozygous recessive offspring.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: How is natural selection different from selective breeding?
options: In natural selection the environment determines which individuals survive
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Nature selects for survival; humans select for features useful to them.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: What do natural selection and selective breeding have in common?
options: Both need variation and change allele frequency over generations
Both are carried out by humans
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Both act on existing variation, over many generations.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why does selective breeding of fish for fast growth work?
options: Alleles for fast growth are passed on to the offspring
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Breeding the fastest growers means their alleles for fast growth are passed on and become more common.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Why does cattle height vary over a smooth range while hair colour has only three types?
options: Hair colour is affected by diet
Height is polygenic and affected by the environment
Height is controlled by one gene
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Many genes plus the environment give a continuous range; one gene gives a few clear types.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: A field of genetically very similar wheat is wiped out by a new disease. Why?
options: Little variation — no plants had an allele to resist it
The disease was caused by selective breeding
17-selection-and-evolution.explain: Low genetic variation means no individuals are likely to be resistant.

17-selection-and-evolution.q: Wheat yield rose from 2.8 to 6.7 tonnes per hectare. What is the percentage increase?
Hares with white fur are more common where there is snow for most of the year. Which explanation is correct?
options: Hares turn white because they are cold
White hares are camouflaged, so survive and reproduce more, passing on alleles for white fur
Snow causes mutations for white fur
